Paterfamilias (beam- ingly): "Thank heaven, my daughter has got a soesible husband, anyhow." A 'Dueller., questioninig little boys about the graduation in the scale of intelligence, asked: • What comes next to lean?" Whereupon one little shaver, who was evidently smarting under A sense of previous defeat, immediately dis- tanced alt competitors by promptly shouting, "His flannel shirt, ma'am !" BRITISII husbands, when their dinner parties turn out failures, are apt to grumble at their wives for the cook's misdemeanours, but they abstain from the practical style of rebuking practised by the celestial.. Recently the Chinese professor at a university gave a national banquet to fellow pro- fessors, and was much put out because the cookery was not to his taste. After a time he got up, bowed solemnly, said, "Go lickee wife," and departed, returning presently, smiling as blandly as nails', after having administered judicious chas- tisement to his better half.

The other day he brought his sister in to dinner and gave her a general intro- duction somewhat as follows 'Ladies and gentle- men, this is my sister.' Then he electrified the gathering by continuing : 'My sister, these are ladies and gentlemen. Whereat the ladies and gentlemen present were highly delighted at such an indorsement.

TIM following anecdote is reported from Dtlr- . Some sheep belonging to a farmer named Reed having been stolen in the neighbourhood of a colliery village, a local preacher, having • col- iection to make, thought he would turn the event to good account, so he said: "We have a col- iection to make this morning, and I hope whoever was so wicked as to steal Mr. Reed's sheep won't put anything on the plate." The collection was the largest ever taken in the place. " ALL a woman asks is to be loved," says a „gushing poet. Then all this stuff about her want- ing new bonnets and jewellery must be a vile -elander. ;Virg : " Why, Henry, the dinner is spoiled. Where have you been ? ' Suburbanite: "I got carried past the station, and had to wait an hour for the up-train." Wife : " Reading at the time, I suppost ! " Suburbanite : "No ; I was trying to convince a friend of the Denefits of living in the suburbs." ---

SLMEON EASYGO, after living sixty years on a farm, finds his quarters on shipboard somewhat cramped. Ho obviates the lack of space, however, by stowing his garments and shoe.s into a round aperture in the side of the vessel on going to bed. 7 a.m.—Startling disclosures: "Steward, last night I put my clothes in that there cupboard, and they ain't there now." "That ain't a cupboard; that's a porthole, sir." HUSBAND: "Why do your clothes coat you twenty pounds more this year than they did last? Aren't things cheaper?" Wife: "Yes, dear; that's just it. There are so many more bargains." "Now, papa, tell me what is humbug?" questioned the ten-year-old son of a friend of ours. •• It is," replied the father, "when your mother pretends to be very fond of me and puts no buttons on my shirt." "BROMLEY, here's an account of a woman who lived forty-eight days on water." " That's nothing, Derringer. My father has been living on water for the last ten years." "Do you expect me to believe that, eh? Why don't you add that be grew fat on it?" "Well, he did. He's a sea captain." " Skin maker and seller (portnia.uteatt shop)." " Ladies furnished in the upstairs." A VOLUNTEER, who was a great man in his own eyes, was by some influence appointed captain. He could hardly speak of anything but his new dignity. Meeting a friend one day he accosted thim thus :—" Well, Jim, I suppose you know 1 have been appointei captain?" "Yes,' said .lilo, I heard so." "Well, what do you folks say about it ? " asked the captain. "They don't say nothin," replied truthful James, "they just laugh." PurrristG Him EIGHT. —A stranger, just rrived at a boardinghouse whose table and boarders he found not at all to his liking, fell into conversation with a quiet looking lady who sat near him in the dining-room. "I say," said he softly, "have you been a prisoner long in this—this menagerie '!" "[l'm :" said the lady; " prisoner ' isn't exactly the word in my case. You see, I'm the andlady, and it's I who feed the animals ! " AN amateur dramatic company gave a per- formance a few nights ago. The piece was ". Hamlet," and Gus Snobberly played the Ghost. Gus expressed his lack of confidence in himself, but the manager reassured him by Baying: "Now, Gus, all in the world you have to do is to come in and say, lam thy father's grost,' anti you must do it in a deep, sonorous voice." Gus said he would try and do his level beat. When the ghost's turn came, he spoiled the tragic effect of the wt cle performance by Haying : " I am thy fa ,lie's ghost, and you must do it in a deep, sonorous voice." A SLIGHT MISUNDERSTANDING.—A clergyman was very anxious to introduce some new hymn- books into the church, and arranged with his clerk that the latter was to give out the notice immedi- ately after the sermon. The clerk, however, had a notice of his own with reference to the baptism nf infants to give out; accordingly, at the close of the sermon he rose and announced that—" All those who had children whom they wished to have baptised were to send in their names at once to the clerk." The clergyman, who was stone deaf, assumed that the clerk w.ts giving out the hymn- book notice, and immediately rose and said : "And I should like to say, for the benefit of those who haven't any, that they may be obtained in the vestry any day from 3 to 4 o'clock; the ordinary little ones at Is. each, and special ones with red backs at Is. 4d,"

Among Mr. Chamberlain's friends there is no secret made of the fact that he is more in favour of prompt inquiry into the doings of the Chartered Company than would be gathered from his speech of Friday, and as the outside feeling that the in- vestigation ought to take place at the earliest possible moment is growing in strength, it is thought not impossible that the Government in- tentions will be expedited.

There was an extraordinary demonstration on I Tuesday morning at the City Temple, which was I more crowded than usual during the address of the I chairman of the Congregational Union. It occurred when Mr. Morlais Jones, alluding to the Education Bill as" The Bishop of London's Bill and the Parish Priests' Bill," declared that Congregational- ists must fight it "to their last breath." This de- claration so excited the vast congregation that they rose to their feet and cheered vehemently for I some seconds,the men waving their hats and ladies their handkerchiefs. Mr. Jones also provoked much applause by his emphatic language in reference to the proposal for reunion, which he described as a mere chimera, and as the dream of the picnic party at Grindelwaid. Thera was one thing,he said,which above all others made it impossible for Congrega- tionalists to find their home in the Establisbed Church, and that was the part the priest plays in it. Archbishop Laud lived in an army of priests and laymen still. "Mr. Athelstan Rileyy," pro- ceeded the chairman, amid much hiesing, "is a lineal descendant of Laud. The spirit of his ances- tor, the Archbishop, is in him," and be added, amid renewed cheers," the Church in which the priest is master can b 6 no home for us."

It is practically certain that the Government will drop clause 27 of the Education Bill—the clause which allows religious instructors of the various denominations to enter the schools. But at present the Government adhere firmly to the clauses which fix limits to the Parliamentary grant and enable municipal authorities to dishonour the demand notes of school boards. It is probable that the Government will yield on the point of the personnel of the new local authority, so that it will become incumbent on county and county borough councils to appoint as members of the authority persons experienced in the management of schools and in teaching.

The interview with President Kruger,which was reported in Tuesday's papers, puts the South African question in a new aspect, and incalculably increases Mr. Chamberlain's difficulty. It is clear that he has no intention of letting his prisoners out of his control so long as Mr. Rhodes is, I will not say at large, but at least is made a hero and lion of by influential men at home, is excused by Mr. Cha- mberlain, and relegated to South Africa by the Government of this country to prosecute a career at once Imperial and personal. The President's claim amounts almost to a demand, for it is some- thing more than a suggestion, not only that Mr. Rhodes and those who engineered the company should be punished,but that the company's charter should either be modified or abolished. Members on both sides of the House acknowledge that the President has created a situation of great delicacy, which leaves Mr. Chamberlain practically on the horns of a dilemma from which the utmost finess- ing of diplomacy will be required to extricate him.

The members of the House of Commons had on Wednesday their first opportunity of witnessing a picturesque spectacle, not unfamiliar to their older colleagues, although of somewhat infrequent occur- rence. This was the apparition of the Lord Mayor of Dublin, who, taking advantage of the privilege enjoyed only by the Corporations of Dublin and London of presenting petitions at the bar, came down in full State panoply, wearing scarlet and ermine, with a blazoned retinue of mace beater, sword bearer, city marshal, sheriffs, and aldermen, all fearfully and wonderfully clad and alarmingly armed. The weapons and large part of the follow- ing were left in the outer courts. When, on sten- torian announcement by the head doorkeeper, the Lord Mayor advanced to the bar, with a tall sheriff on one hand, and on the other a short town-clerk, looking As it in the custody of the Sergeant- at-Arms, who stood besides them severely watchful, the mace on his shoulder, " Lord Mayor, what have you there?" demanded the Speaker, with dignity, but without quite emulating the awe-inspiring tones which Mr. Speaker Peel was wont on such occasions to infuse terror into ' the hearts of the suppliants. The many paged document which the Lord Mayor, thus invoked, proceeded to unfold and to read in nervous accents, and with visibly trembling hands, proved to be an appeal to Parliament for the amnesty of all Irish political offenders. The Lord Mayor was amusing- ly embarrassed by the necessity of managing the tall silver wand held in his left hand what time he had to turn over the leaves of his petition. His town-clerk, however, came to his assistance, and performed the office customary to swains hanging over some fair performer on the piano. The terms of the petition having been duly recited, the repre- sentatives of the Corporation of Dublin withdrew with profound obeisances, and remained for some time the centre of attraction in the lobby, which for the occasion bloomed like a bed of scarlet geraniums.

The reduction in the number of ships composing the Flying Squadron by upwards of a half, and the prospect of the remaining vessels being ordered at an early date to rejoin other squadrons, indicate the close ot a chapter in our foreign relations. The rquadron may be regarded as having been a demon- stration directly' against Germany, which it re- minded of its powerlessness to carry out any openly offensive operation against this country. To this • fact, and the necessities of the Triple Alliance, coupled with the entire collapse of the Jameson raid,we owe the preservation of the European peace. It taught the Emperor that if he wished to proceed against this country in South Africa it must be by concealed and insidious means, and not by open hostility; and one of the most pregnant facts in connection with Mr. Chamberlain's great speech on Friday was his pointed reference, twice over, to our power in South Africa being in course of undermining from without. This had no mean- ing except in its application to Germany.

Large as the Ministerial majority was on the second reading of the Education Bill, it would have been still larger if all the Unionists had supported the Government. There were, however, some eighteen absentees unpaired. About eight of these are supposed to be accounted for by absence abroad, one or two being at present in South Africa. But at least an equal number were away without any special reason, except, apparently, distrust of the principle of the bill. Mr. George Dixon, for in- stance, did not vote, nor did Sir John Lubbock. Among the other Liberal Unionists who stayed away were Mr. A. Cross, Mr. Cameron Corbett, and Sir Thomas Lea. When the Hottge gets into com- mittee on the bill it is probable that the full extent of the Liberal Unionist objection to its provisions will become much clearer than it has been hitherto.

The chief event in Dr. C. A. Berry% career, which will interest the general public hearing of his elec- tion to the chairmanship of the Congregational Union, is the fact that he was offered and declined the pulpit of the late Henry Ward Beecher. The decision gave great satisfaction to Dr. Berry's influential congregation in Wolverhampton, where he has been a force for several years on the side of progress. Possessed ofa strong clear voice, and imbued with a deep faith in Nonconformity, Dr. Berry is an admirable chairman elect, chosen at such a time as this, when the need of such a man in the forefront is undoubted.

THINGS A WOMAN WANTS TO KNOW.

Now that cycling is all the rage, ana popularity is ever on the increase, I feel that I cannot do better than devote my attention to this all-important subject this week. One hears it said on all sides that an absolutely perfect cycling skirt has yet to be invented, and, when one sees the numerous awkward and full skirts which are only too often seen nowa- days, one really feels inclined to agree that improvement is possible in this direction.• There is nothing better for a cycling skirt than one which just clears the ankles. It must be plainly made, with rather a wide front gore. and should not measure more than two and three-quarteroyards round the bottom. The front breadth should be lined with silk, or some material with a silky surface, so that the skirt will not ride up over the knees. Personally, I prefer a skirt lir.ed throughout, is I think the additional weight helps to keep it in place. There are others, however, who disagree with me on this point, so evidently it is a question for every lady to decide for herself. A skirt as short as this needs no braid; indeed a skirt braid is one of the most danger- ous things with which a lady cyclist can have
To be had from PATTERN DEPARTMENT, 18, HENRIETTA STREET, LONDON, W.C.

anything to do. She should be careful, too, that her skirt hem is firmly hemmed or stitched, so that there is no possibility of its catching in the treadle, when, undoubtedly, the skirt would become entangled, and she would be thrown.

With regard to the bodice, or coat, choose a Norfolk jacket. Let it be simply and neatly made to button down the centre of the front, with a fold on either side. The back must be plain, with a similar fold down the centre. I think this is neater than the two or three folds with which some people ornament the backs of their Norfolk coats.

Let the sleeves be of moderate dimensions, and the cuffs finished neatly to admit the shirt cuffs. The lining of a Norfolk jacket should be thin, for at this time of the year especially the coolest of garments should be ours for cycling. Choose, therefore, a thin silk or polonaise, a material which can be bought from any good draper. .It is produced in a variety of shot shades, and has the appearance of silk, the price of it being only 114 d. a yard. I can tell you from previous experience that this is a material which wears exceedingly well. It is the fashion this year to wear leather belts with Norfolk jackets, so I advise you to copy this detail. Some ladies like to wear a blouse when cycling, and when this is the case choose one of the neatest possible style. Nothing at all flyaway, or trimmed with lace,
To be had from PATTERN DEPARTMVNT„ 18, HENRIETTA STREET, LONDON, W.C.

looks well on a bicycle, or is indeed suitable to it. Sometimes, of course, one is glad to use one's machine to ride out to a tennis party or picnic, and in that case a pretty and neat blouse will be found very useful. Let me draw your attention to the design for a blouse on this page. It is intended to be carried out in a pretty spotted cambric, and is made with a simple, full bodice, with a box- pleat down the centre of the front, and two cape collars on the shoulders. A high collar with turn-down points over, and cuffs to match, complete this dainty little garment. When making your bicycle skirt, let me advise you to omit the back placquet-hole, and instead, have one under the left front seam. This can be easily managed, and I find it best to put the buttons on to the front gore, and the buttonholes beneath. In this way the skirt is kept absolutely neat in the front. , The pocket-hole in a cycling shirt should be let into the right front seam. Pocket or placquet-holes at the back, or towards the back, are very apt to catch in the saddle in mounting, in which case a bad throw is likely to be the result. This arrangement of the placquet hole allows of another arrangement which I consider good for a skirt to be worn with blouses, and which is, namely, to stitch the waistband on to the band of the skirt at the back from one front 'seam to the other. In this way there is no possibility of the skirt dropping an:l show- int, a gap between the waistband and the skirt, a 'disaster which would condemn even the smartest and best made costume., _ _ . .

Another point which is a difficlay to some ladies, is how to make the hat st iy firndy on the head. For ordinary riding there is nothing More comfortable than a sailor hat of moderate brim, worn with an elastic round the knot of hair at the back. Twist a hairpin round the elastic, and then into the hair, and in this way the hat will be made perfectly firm, even in the roughest wind. Now that the hair is worn so high, and is fairly fluffy, the elastic is scarcely noticeable, and the comfort of it is great.

Willow-pattern ribbon is the very latest idea. This is being extensively used to make the big bows so much worn on hats. I+L w there is very little doubt the willow i pattern with its quaint legend s very nice on plates and dishes, but on bats it looks stiff and inconsistent. It is however quite of the new and prevalent shade of blue.

The opening of the Covent Garden Opera Season last Monday was as successful as it could well be. With bright June weather outside, a house overflowing with the elite of the London season, with Royalty in the boxes, and Gounod's delicious 11,)meo and Juliet, the opening night ot May 11th, 1896 will be memorable for years to come. The Duchess of Fite, wearing her magnificent diamonds occupied her usual box, and Lady de Grey wore her famous pearls. In the stalls I noticed the young Duchess of Marlborough exquisitely dreased,look- ing very bright and animated.

It seems that up to the present moment no town resi- dence has been fixed upon for Prince Carl of Denmark and Princess Maud,who when married purpose spending a portion of each year in London. There is some talk of the Queen making over the palace at Kew to the young couple, but no decision in the matter has yet been arrived at. Kew, of course, is not quite London, but it is very near, and Princess Maud would be within easy distance of her sister, the Duchess of Fife, at East Sheen. It is a picturesque, red brick mansion, dating back to the reign of James 11., is in good repair and most pleasantly situated overlooking the river and the Ros al gardens.

The Amateur Alt Exhibition, annually held for the benefit of various deslrving London charities, and which is now open to the public at No. I, Belgrave- square, the residence of Mr. Reuben Sassoon, who has lent his mansion for the art season, deserves special mention.as it contains two pictures by royal ladies. The Princess of Wales has sent a sea piece in water colours. It is a simple scene by the sea shore of some little fish- ing village, and is a wonderfully clever study, evidently taken direct from Nature. The Marchioness of Lorne has sent a single head called "A Pifferrare Boy." There is no doubt Princess Louise is an artist of exceptional at- tainments, and had this picture been sent anonymously to the Royal Academy, it would in all probability have been accepted and hung on the line. Speaking of the &caderny reminds me that this year's exhibition contains one ye'', charming water colour by the well-known throat specialist, Dr. Lennox Browne. Dr. Erowne is well known to be a very busy man, but it seems he has found time to paint charming little views ot Thames scenery. This id,tiowever,the first year he has attained the distinction of having a picture exhibited at Burling- ton House.

Wile. Roes Bonheur, one of whose superb animal pic- tures.that ef a rough sheep docis just now to be seen in the form of an engraving in many London shops, in ap- pearance somewhat reaembles a Norman parish priest. She is short and somewhat stout, dresses very plainly. and is about 70 years at age. She boa been a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour since 1865. There is no doubt Mdlle. Rosa Bonheur's family possess artistic taste to an unusual degree. Her father,her Aster, her brothers.and several of their relatives and descendants have displayed remarkable ability in painting, or sculpture, or both. Mdlle. Bonheur's only piece of sculpture is a little marble figure of a ram of which the desi4n and work- manship are quite goed enough to provoke the wish that she had been able to pursue the two arts instead of hav- ing confined her energies to one. Lady Angela St. Clair Erskine, whose marriage hag recently taken place, is the youngest daughter of Blanche, Countess of Rosalyn. Lady Rosslyn was twice married, the beautiful Countess of Warwick being one of her dau4hters by her firat marriage and the equally lovely Ductless of Sutherland by the oth 1. union. All these ladies are most energetic in tne cause of charity. Lady Rosslyn started and maintains a convalescent home for poor mothers.the Denham of Sutherland has founded a nursing charity in the Highlands, and the Countess of Warwick has for years been the source from which the Easton School of Fine Needle work has obtained its strength. Another American millionaire's is shortly to be con- verted into an" Old World Princess." Miss Miluas.who by the way has a dowry of two millions sterling, is a sister of Mrs. Eugene Kelly, one of the richest women in the world. The happy man is Prince Albert Radziwell, a Pole. It appears the Radziwells are rather give" to making good matches from a financial point of view,ene of them married the rich daughter of M. Blanc, the founder of Monte Carlo.

An immense am omit of trouble is just now being ex- pended upon belts. The most extravagant are in white kid, jewelled with turquoises. Very attractive speci- mens are being made of plain scarlet leather, fastened in front with • at gold ornament. Kid belts of all colors traced with sequins are to be seen, but them are only be- coming to slim figures. Black kid forms the foundation of many of the newest belts this being usually treated with gold sequins and imitation turquoise and emeralds. Quite a popular gift at the present moment is the jewel- led clasp, which, to be correct, must fasten the plain white leather belt in front. Toques are to be larger and of a different shape to those of last season. At the private view at Burlington House, I noticed one, worn by a well-known saciety woman, in back course chip, bent about in all directions but apparently there was method in its madnes., for on the head it was most becoming. It was trimmed with a cluster of white quill feathers tipped with black and pinned in with a cluster of Parisian diamonds, while at the other side there was a small bunch of crimson roses with their own foliage.-- This all sounds very simple, but I happen to know that it was an especially expensive model from a nioit exclusive milliner. The evar increasing use of the bicycle, coupled with the certain advent of the horseleas carriage, is having a decided effect already in the West End of London. One large livery-stable keeper having found the season's orders very small, owing to the substitution of the iron horse for the living ene, as a faahionable means of exer- cise, has recently gives up his business. By the way the exparts of cycles last year amounted to the value of £1,393,810, as against £1,200,913 the year before. But this year the tide is rising bighei still. Tube makers are employed incessantly on cycle materials, and chain makers cannot complete their orders, so overwhelmed are they, with them. , A novel plan was hit upon by a gentleman a few days back when applying for a summons sgsinst a cabdriver who had driven in such a way as to injure his bicycle. A rough sketch was handed by the cyclist to the magis- trate who however decided it was not a case for his court. It was obvious that if the point was to be settled by a sketchiboth sides would have to be represented in the sketching competition. The indignant applicant ob- served that "cabdrivers were really the terror of cyclists." 'Time was when cyclists went with bated breath only too grateful if cabmen or coachmen re- frained from driving over them, but now we have changed all that, and it seems as though cyclists will soon be demanding, as Mr. Punch has augrsted. that every cab shall be preceded by a man with a red flag. " A Chaperon Cyclists' Association " which provides companions for those who do not think it correct to ride alone and who cannot find friends to ride with them is the very latest idea in connection with the bicycle craze. The qualification for the chaperon are said to be that she should be an experienced rider and either a married or a widow lady. The terms are 3.5. 61. an hour or 10i. BJ. per day,the chaperon finding her own cycle. Now it seems to me that taking into consideration the fact that accidents to women cyclists are of constant occurrence, a course of study in " first aid "added to the chaperon's list of accomplishments would be a distinct advantage. ALMOND PUDDING is delicious. Blanch and pound two ounces of sweet almonds, heat them in t pint of milk, mix in ilb. of mashed potatoes, Vb. of butter, three eggs, and the rind and juice of one lemon. Beat alto- gether and bake for half an hour in a greased pie dish. " MADGE."

div.head: HIDDEN HAND;
div.p: THE HIDDEN HAND;
OR. CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. Dr .MIZS. E. D. E. N. SOUTUWOUTIL
CHAPTER XXXVII.

CAP'S RETURN. "Must / give way and room for your rash choler Shall I be frighted when a madman stares? Go show your slaves how choleric you are! And make your bondsmen tremble! I'll not blench.' —SHAKESPY.ARE. It happened that about sunrise that morning, Wool awoke in the cellar, and remembered that upon the night previous his master had com- manded him to sally forth in the storm and seek his young mistress, and had forbidden him, on pain of broken bones, to return withottt bringing her safe. Therefore, what ..id the honest soul do but to steal out to the stables, saddle and mount a horse, and ride back to the house just as Mrs. Condiment had come out into the poultry-yard to get eggs for breakfasit. " Missus Compliment. ma'am, I'se been out all night in search of Mies Caterpillar, without finding of her. Is she come back, ma'am?" "Lor no, indeed, Wool. I'm very anxious, and the Major is taking on dreadful. But I hope she is safe in some house. But, poor Wool, you must have had a dreadful time out all night in the storm, looking for her." "Awful, Missus Compliment, ma'am, awful I" said Wool.
"Indeed, I know you had, my poor creature. C)me in and get 801118 warm breakfast," said the

kind old I kdyt "I daren't, Missus Compliment. Old marso forbid me to show my face to him until I fetch Miss Caterpillar home safe," said Wool, turning his horse's head as if to go. In doing so, he saw Capitola galloping towardo the house, and with an exclamation of joy, pointed her out to the old lady, and rode on to meet her. _ _ _

"Oh, Miss Caterpillar,. Tee so glad I've found you. 180 done been out looking for you all night long!" exclaimed Wool, as he met her. Capitola pulled up her horse, and surveyed the speaker with a comical expression, sayins : " 'Been out all night looking for me? Well, I must say you seem in a fine state of preservation for a man who has been exposed to the storm all night. You have not a wet thread on you !" " Ler, Miss, it rained tilt one o'clock, and then the wind riz and blowed till, six, and blowed me dry ! ' said Wool, as he sprang off his horse and helped his young mistress to alight. Then, instead of taking the beasts to the stable, he tied them to the tree, mud hurried into the house, and up stairs to his master's room, to apprise him of the return of the lost sheep, Capitola. Old Hurricane was lying awake, tossing, groan. ing and grumbling with anxiety.. On seeing Wool enter, he deliberately raised up and seized a heavy iron candlestick, and held it ready to hurl at the head of that worthy, whom he thus addressed: .
Ah, you have come, you, atrocious villain. You know the conditions If yen have dared to show your face without bringing, your young mis- tress —"

"Please, marse-, I wur out looking for her all night f" "Have you brought her theeidered Old Hur- ricane, rising up. " Please, marse, yes, sir. I done found her and brought her home safe." "send her up to me," said 04d!Hurricane, sink- ing back with a sigh of infinite relief. Wool flew to do his bidding. In five minutes Capitol& entered her uncle's chamber. _ _ _ _

Now OM Hurricane had spent a night of almost intolerable anxiety upon his favourite's account, bewailing her danger and praying for her safety; but no sooner did he see her enter his chamber safe and sound, and smiling„ than indignation quite mastered him, and jumping out of the bed in his nigntgown, he made a dash straight at Capitola. Now, had Capitols run, there is little doubt but that, in the blindness of his fury,: he would have caught and beat her then and there.. But Cap saw him coming, drew up her tiny form, folded her arms, and looked him directly in the lace. This stopped him, but like a. mettlesome old horse suddenly pulled up in full career, he stamped, and reared, and plunged with fury, and foamed, and spluttered, and stuttered before he could get words out. "What do you mean, you vixen, by standing there and popping your great grey eyes out at me? Are you going to bite, you tigress? What do you mean by facing me at all ?" he roared, shaking his fist within an inch of Cs.pitola's little pug nose. "I am here because you sent for me, sir," was Cap's unanswerable rejoinder. " ' Here because I sent for yen!' humph ! humph! humph! and come dancing and smiling into my room as if you had not kept me awake all the live long night—yes ! driven me within one inch of a brain fever! Not that I cared: for you, you limb of Old Nick ! not that I cared for you, except to wish with all my heart and soul that something or other had happened to you, you vagrant ! Where did you spend the night, you lunatic?' "At the Hidden House, where I went to make a call on My new neighbour. Ills& Day, and where I was caught iu the storm." "I wish to heaven you had been caught in a man-trap and had all your limbs broken, you—you —you - Omi !" ejaculated Old Hurricane, turning short and trotting up and down the room. Pre- sently he stopped before Capitals, and rapping his cane down upon the floor, demanded : " Wiio diu you see at-that accursed place, you— you—you infatua.ed mania. ?" "Miss Day, Mr. Le Noir, Mrs. Knight, awl a man-servant name unknown," coolly replied Cap. "And the head demon, where was he ?" ",Uncle, if by the head demon you mean Old Nick, I think it quite likely, from present appear- ances, that he passed the night at Hurricane "1 mean—Colonel Le Noir!" exclaimed Old Hurr cane, as if the name choked him.
"O: ! I understand that he had that day left home." Umph ! Oh I Ah ! that accounts for it," mut-
tered Old Hurricane to himself—then, seeing Cap- Rola was wisifully reg:trding his face, and attend- ing to his muttered phrases, he broke out upon her with :

Get out of th's—this—" he meant to say get out of this house," but a sure instinct warned him that if he should speak thus, Capito!a., unlike the ot..er members of his household, would take him at his word. _
"Get out of this room, you vagabond," he vociferated.
And Cap, with a curtsey vnd a kiss of her hand, danced away.
Old H .rricare stamped up and down the floor, gesticulating like a demoniac, and vociferating: "She'll get herself burked, kidnapped, mur- dered, or wnat not! I'm sure she will! I know

. - tt ! I feel it It's no 1180 to order her not to go; she would be sure to disobey ! and go ten times as often, for the very reason that she was forbidden What the demon shall I do?— Wool! Wool! Wool, you brimstone villain, come her! I" he roared, going to the bell-rope and pulling it until he broke it down. Wool ran in with his hair bristling, his teeth chattering, and his eyes starting. "Come here to me, you varlet! Now listen: You are to keep a sharp look-out after your young mistress. Whenever she rides abroad you are to mount a horse and ride after her, and keep Your eyes open, for if you only once lose sight of her, you knave, do you know what I shall do to you,

eh?" "N —n—no, marse," stammered Wool, pale with apprehension. "1 should cut your eyelids off to improve your vision! Look to it, sir, for I shall keep my word. And now -come and help me to dress," concluded Old Hurricane. Wool, with chattering teeth, shaking knees, and trembling fingers, as isted his master :n his morn- ing t-ilet, meditating the while whether it were no., better to avoid impending dangers by running away.. And, in fact, between his master and his mis- tress, Wool had a hot time of it. The weather, after the storm had cleared the atmosphere, was delightfui, and Cap rode out that very day. Poor Wool kept his eyeballs metaphorically'" skinned," for fear they should be treated literally so—held his eyes wide open, lest Old Hurricane should keep his word, and make it. impossible for him ever to shut them. When Cap stole out, mounted her horse and rode away, in five minutes from the moment of starting she heard a horse's hoofs behind her, and presently saw Wool gallop to her s de. At first Cap bore this good-humouredly enough, only saying: "Go home, Wool, I don't want you. I had much rather ride alone." To_whiett the groom

" It is ole manse's orders, Miss, as I should wait on you." Capitola's spirit rebelled against this ; and sud- denly turning upon her attendant, she indignantly exclaimed : 'Wool, I don't want you, sir 1 I insist upon being left alone and I order you to go home, sir !" Upon this Wool burst into tears and roared. Much surprised, Capitola inquired of him what the matter was. For some • ime, Wool could only reply by sob- bing, but when he was able to articulate he blub- bered forth : "It's 'fluff to make anybody go put his head underneaf of a mea.-ax, so it is 1" "What is the matter, Wool r again inquired Capitols.. " How'd you like tow have your eyelids cut oil'?" howled Wool, indignantly " What f' inT ired Capitola. 'Yes, I axes how'd you like to have your eyelids cut off Case that's what ole marse t'reatens to do long o' me, if I don't follow arter you and keep you in. sight I—And now 7ou forbids of rne to do it, and—and—l'll go and put my head right under- neaf of 04 meat-ax !" Now Capitola was really kind-hearted, and well knowing the despotic temper of her guardian, she pitied Wool, and after a little hesitation, she said:

"Wool,. so your old master says if you don't keep your eyes on me, he'll cut your eyelids off ?" " e—ye--yes. Miss," sobbed Wool. "Did he say if you don't listen, to me he'd cut your earn off?" " N—n—no, Miss." "Did he swear if you didn't talk to me he'd cat your tongue out ?" " N—n—noi Minn." "Well, now,, stop howling, and listen to me. Since at the peril of your eyelids you are obliged to keep me in sight, I give you leave to ride just within view of me; but no nearer, and you are never to let me see or hear you, if you can help it,. for I like to be-alone."

"fit do anything in the world for peace, Miss Caterpillar," said poor Wool. And upon this basis the affair was finally settled. And no douht Capitola owed much. of her personal safety to the fact that Wool kept his eyes open. While these scenes were going on. at Hurricane Hall, momentous events were taking place else- where, which require another chapter for their development.
CITA:FMB XXXVIII.
ANOTHER MY9TERY AT THE HIDDEN HOUSE.
" Hark ! what a, shriek was that of fear intense, Of horror and amazement! What fearful struggle to the door, and thence,
With mazy double, to the casement. !"

An hour after the departure of Capitola' Colonel Le Noir returned to the Hidden House, and learned, from his man David, that upon the preceding evening a young girl, of whose- name he was ignorant, had sought shelter from the storm and passed the night at the mansion. Now Colonel Le Noir was extremely jealous of receiving strangers under his roof—never during his short stay at the Hidden House going out into company, lest he should be obliged in return to entertain visitors. And when: he learned that a strange girl had spent the night beneath his roof, he frowningly directed that Dorcas should be sent to him.
When his morose manager made her appearance, he harshly demanded the name of the young wo- man she had dared to receive beneath his roof.

Now, whether there is any truth in the theory of magnetism or not,. it is certain. that Dorcas Knight, stern,, harsh, reisolute woman that she was towards all others, became as submiseime as a child In the presence•of. Colonel Le Noir... At his commands he gave him all the-information he required, not even withholding the fact of Capitola's strange story of having seen the appa- rition of the pale-faced lady in her chamber, toge- ther with the subsequent discovery of the loss of her ring. Colonel Le•Noir sternly reprimanded his domestic manager for her neglect of. his orders, and dismissed her from his presence. The remainder of the day was passed by him in moody thought. That evening he summoned his son to a private conference iathe parlour—an event that happily delivered poor Clara. Day from their presence at her fireside.. That night Clara, dreading- lest at the end of their interview they might return to her society, retired early to her chamber, where she sat read- ing until a late hour, when she went to bed and found transient forgetfulness of trouble in seep. She did not know how long she had slept, when she was suddenly and terribly awakened by a woman's shriek sounding from the room imme- diately overhead, in which,. upon the night pre- vious, Capitola had slept. Starting up.in bed, Clara, listened.. The shriek wasrepeated—prolonged and piercing, and was accompanied by a muffled sound of strug- gling that shook. the-ceiling overhead. InstinctiveTy springing from her bed, Clara threw on her dressin.;-gown and flew- to.the door, but jest as she turned the latch to open it, she heard a bolt slipped on. the•outside and found herself a prisoner in her own.chamber. Appalled, she stood and listened. Presently there came a sound of footsteps on the- stairs and a. heavy. mmffied noise as of some dead weight being dragged down the staircase and along the passage Then she heard the hall door cautiously opened, and shut. And finally she distinguished the sound. of wheels rolling away from the house.
Unable longer to, restrain herself, she rapped and beat upon, her ow u door, crying aloud for de- liverance.
Presently the bolt was withdrawn, the door jerked open and Dorcas Knit:ht, with a face of horror, stoo(1 before her.

"What is the matter? Who was that scream- ing I'. In the name of mercy what has happened r cried Clara, shrinking in abhorence from the .ghastly woman. " ! it is nothing! there were two tom- cats screaming and fighting in the attic, and they fo• ght all the way down stairs, rolling over and over each other. I've just turned them out," faltered the woman, shivering as with an ague fit. "What—what was that—that went away in the earria_e r asked Clara, shuddering.

"The Colonel, gone to meet the euidy stage at Tip Top, to take him to Washington. He would have taken leave of you last night, but when he ea.i.e to your parlour you had left it." "But—but--there is blood upon your hand, Dorcus Knight !" cried Clara, shaking with horror. "I—l know—the cats scratched me as I put them out," stammered the stern woman, trembling almost as much as Clara herself. These answers failed to satisfy the young girl, who shrank in terror and loathing from that wo- man's presence, and sought the privacy of her own Out,. her, murmuring : "What Ems happened? What has been done, oh heaven! 0, heaven, have mercy on us some dreadful deed has been done in this house to- night !" There was no more sleep for Clara. She heard the clock strike every hour from one to six in the morning, when she arose and dressed herself and went from her loom, expecting to see upon the flodr and walls, and upon the faces ot the house- hold, signs of some dreadful tragedy enacted upon the previous night. But all things were as usual—the same dark, gloomy and neglected magnificence about the rooms and p issages, the same reserved, sullen and silent aspect about the persons. Dorcas Knight presided as usual at the head of the breakfast table, and Craven Le Noir at the foot. Clara sat in her accustomed seat at the side, midway between them. Clara shuddered in taking her cup of coffee from the hand of Dorcas, and declined the wing of fowl that Craven Le Noir would have put upon her pate. Not a word was said upon the subject of the my stcry of the preceding night, until Craven Le Noir, without venturing to meet the eyes of the young girl, said , "You look very pale, Clara !" "Miss Day was frightened by the cats last night," said Dcreas. Clara answered never a word. The ridiculous story essayed to be palmed off upon her credulity in explanation of the night's mystery had not gained an instant's belief. She knew that the cry that had startled her from sleep, had burst in 6trong agony from human lips. That the helpless weight she had heard dragged down the stairs and along the whole length of the passage, was some dead or insensible human form ! , That the blood she had seen upon the hand of Dorcas Knight, was—oh, heaven, her mind shrank back appalled with horror, at the thought which she dared not entertain! She could only shudder, pray and trust in. God. (To be contintsid.)

div.head: NEEDLESS ALARM.
div.p: NEEDLESS ALARM.

Whether the suffering which people undergo from dis- ease is more physical than mental is a point not easy to decide. It depends largely on the nature of the disease, and the make-up of the individual. Experience seem to show, however, that in one prevailing disease—indi- gestion or dyspepsia, the two kinds of suffering are very evenly divided, and both very great, the mental distress being chiefly due to the illusions and deceptions which attend it. For example, though dyspepsia is solely an affection of the digestive organs it has power to set up disorders in others which always alarm the sufferer, and often perplex his medical advisers. These symptoms or sequences may relate to the head., the. heart, the sight, the hearing, the lungs, or to other organs or. functions. Take an illustration or two.

"In the spring of 1891," says Mr. Edward Tatham, I fell into a low, weak state of health. I bad a foul taste in my mouth, and was constantly [spitting up a thick phlegm. My appetite was poor and after eating I had fulness and pain at the chest—the latter seemed to be puffed or swollen. What made me most anxious was my breathing, which came to be se difficult and short that at times I could only catch my bteath by an effort. I was led to fancy that something must ail my lungs, especially as so great a quantity of muscus gathered in my throat and mouth. It was usually worse at night, and 1 got very little sleep en account of it; sometimes none at all. In the morning I was quite worn out.

"As time went on I became very weak,and was much, put to it to get about. I took all kinds of medicines and got no proper relief from anything. In February, 1893, Mr. William Beardsley, grocm, Cotmanhay, told me how he had been cured of a like trouble by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. Acting on his advice I got a bottle of this medicine from Mr. Platt's Dru g Stores Awsworth Road. and alter taking it felt quite another man. My breathing was min, and my food agreed with me. I continued using the Syrup,and got stronger and better every day. When I had taken four bottles I was as well as ever,being free from all pain or discom- fort. My wife, who has suffered, for years from liver complaint, has taken the Syrup with the same good re- sults as in my own case. You are at liberty to make any use you like of this statement (Signed) Edward Tatham, Tatham's Lane, Cotmanhay Road, Ilkeston, Derbyshire, March 21st, 189 E." "In October, 1888," writes another, "I began to feel weak, heavy, and tired. My appetite was poor, and after eating I had distress at the stomach, tr•gether with shortness of breath, and a good deal of pain across the chest. Sometimes I would.be taken with sudden dizzi- ness, as though I must falbto the ground. Celd,clammy sweats used to break out all over me and I trembled from head to foot. Finally, I got so weak I could scarcely walk to my work. .Indeed, I had occasionally to leave my work; I have been away as long as month at a time. In this way .I suffered for shout two years.

"In August, 1890, Mr, Thompson, the grocer in Church-st reet, urged me to try Mother Seigel's Syrup After taking only one bottle I felt better. My food agreed with me and I was stronger. Continuing with this medicine, gradually all pain left me, and I com- pletely recovered my health. Since then I have kept the Syrup in the house for use in time of need. You are free to publish this statement. (Signed) William •Mallender, 71, Robinson's Buildings, Newhill, Watt; near Sheffield, October llth, 1895."
Cases of supposed diseases of the heart, of the ner- vous system, of the kidoeyerkc., constantly pr)ve to not organic affections .of those , parts at all. but

merely local or functional disturbance; caused by the toxic or poisonous principles thrown into the blood by the decomposition or fermentation of food in the stomach ; otherwise by dyspepsia or indigestion. But until they are discovered to be so they are mistakenly treated ; and serious, often fatal., results follevr. Until pronounced and undeniable symptoms or organic mis- chief show themselves (which is not the case once in a hundred times) you may take it !for granted that your ailment is some form of dysepsia, easily curable by Mother Seigel's Syrup, as demonstrated by the two in- stances cited above.

div.head: PHCENIX PARK _MURDERS.
div.p: THE PHCENIX PARK _MURDERS.

Mr. 'Tighe Hopkins concludes his account of the memories of Kilmainharn Prison, in the May Number of the ''\Winclitor Magazine." Speaking of the death of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. 'Burke, he says "The murder had been carefully and most minutely planned, and the Phcenix Park had been selected as the scene. The Under Secretary has, his official residence is the pack, a little more than a mile.from the main en- trance.. It is opposite to the Cief-Secretary's lodge.and not far .from the Viceregal lodge. The Invincibles were to wait in the park for Mr. Burite..who usually walked or took a hackney car to his house on,leaving his office in the Castle. ,Eleven of them itt all were under orders for the park, but the actual business of the assassination was in the hands of the four whom :Kavanagh was to drive on his outside-car. Since midday they had beeo hearteninwthemselves with whisky,and were all more or less drunk at the hour of starting. All the car party were armed wittrknives. Fallowing the car was the cab driven Fitzharria Skin the Goat') in which were Dan Curley, M. Fagan andloe Hanlon, each furnished .with a loaded revolver. Carey and James Smith, whocompleted the band, were already on the scene. Smith's presence was necessary for A-singular reason. He,and he alone of the party, was able to identify Mr. Burke. 'Tnese men, it is to he remarkech, had nothing in the ,nature of a private wrong to avenge. Not a man amongst them had ever in his lifetime aufered, directly or indirectly., the very smallest injustice at the hands of Mr. Burke. To o:,e and all of them he was a name and .nothing more. :Smith excepted,!they were ignorant even of his appear- ance. At aboatifive minutes past seven smari was seen :to alight from an outside car just within thenpark gates. "'Tie Burke,' Smith said to Carey. • which of them ?' Asked Carey, for .the one which had quitted the car had atopped to speak toanother man on the footpath. Him that's afther gettit'. down.' said Smith. The man in ray.' Mr. Burkeorecognixing Lord Frederick Caven- dish, who was going on foot to his new home in the tpark, bad dismissed his car, and the two etien set out to walk together. Carey signalled Kavanagh with his handkerchief and as the car came up gave the word tol Brady, the Hercules and the party, who, as was wel understood was to do the deed alone. Hind the max, t.gray,' said Carey. None of them knewiloord Frederick Cavendish. Carey and Smith ad- vanced to meet Mr. Burke and Lord Fred-rick, Brady walking on the inside of the path opposite to Mr. Burke. At the instant of meeting, Brady stooped as if to tie his shoe then, rising suddenly, gripped Mr. Burke by the waist, rarung him round,and dealt him one terrific blow in the back. The Hercsale,an Brady did his work well and quickly, for Lord Frederick was in the death throe.; now. igif death he owed to -the fine Flue blood In It was not intended to kill him, but he had turned in- stantly to defend his companion (with an u:rtrrella)And Brady. Bunke being down.grappled with Lord Frederick and str dchirn deep in the breast under the left clavicle. ra One blow Apiece sufficed, ifireugh an opening in the trees Lord Spencer, standinf; with his secretary in a window of thefliceregal Lodge, had watched the scuffle on the path and sent the secretory to inquire what it was. Kawanagtt, waiting quiettlx, with the car turned in the direction in which the flight was to be, hop flick- ing his little browa mare with the wtip to heat her for the start. The four sprang on the car,Kavanagh let out the reins and the mare went away at the gallop."

div.head: CAIRO-STREET NEW t-CHOOLS. OPENING PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: THE CAIRO-STREET NEW t-CHOOLS. OPENING PROCEEDINGS.

On Saturday afternoon the handsome buildings in Cairo-street,which have been erected:by the congregation of the Unitarian Chapel were formally opened for Sun- day School use. From 3.30 to 4 o'clock a dedication service was held in the chapel, conducted by the Revs. H. E. Dawson, B.A. and NV. H. Drummond, B.A. (pastor). There was a good attendance and hymns and prayer appropriate to the occasion were included in the service. At the con- clusion of the service a procession headed by Mr. W. Long and Mrs. Walter M. Shipman, followed by the offi- ciating ministers, the teachers of the Sunday School,and the members of the Chapel Committee, was made to the main entrance of the new schools. where Mrs. Shipman unlocked the door. All then proceeded to the new cop- grega,tional parlour where the opening meeting was held. The loom was crowded and Mr. W. Long, J.P., took the chair. Among the rest present were—Mr. and Mrs. Walter Shipman, Mrs. Long, the Rev. W. H. and Mrs. Drummond, the Rev. H. E. and Mrs. Dawson, the Rev. F. K. Freeston, Mr. and Mrs. W. Owen, Councillor and Mrs. F. W. Monks, Mr. and Mrs. F. Monks. Mr. and Mrs. Rhymer Young, Mr. and Mrs. Young, sen., Mr. and Mrs. T. Birchall, Mr. and Mrs. Thornly kHydel, Mr. and Mrs. A. Holt (Liverpool), Colonel and Mrs. Filcher. M. %V. H. Travers, Rev. J. Armstrong (Liverpool), Rev. Mr. Davies (Liverpool), Rev. Lloyd Jones, (Liverpool), Rev. Mr. Beamont (Gateacre), Rev. H. S. Tayler, M.A. (President of the Manchester District Sunday School Association), Mr. Perris (son of the Rev. H. W. Perris), the Misses Monks, Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Knowles, Mr. Hill (superintendent of Sunday School) and Mrs. Hill, Mr. J. Pemberton (superintendent of the Sunday School)Mr. T. C.Hollings- worth (secretary), Mrs. Perris, Mr. John Houghton (Sankey), Mr. John Houghton (Appleton), Mr. John Gandy. Mr. Whittle, Mr. and Mrs. Andrew L.athbone, Mr. and Mrs. Williams, Mrs. and Miss Williams, Mr. Charles Twiss, Mr. and Mrs. NV. H. Woodcock. Mrs. SHIPMAN in declaring the rooms open said they had all worked for them, ti,ey were all beautiful, and all felt that they would long be known in Warrington as the nicest schools in the town,where the best and freeest thought was taught. (Applause.) The Cinemas/a said that to all Cairo-street people that was a very joyous day. (Hear, hear.) The project of having better accommodation for their children had been long before them ,as they had felt they had not proper accommodation for their work. (Ap- plause.) For as long as some of them could remember the idea of having better accommodation had, he thought, grown and grown ever since the old schools below began to be filled. He could not help thinking just then, how ;much it would have gladdened the hearts of some of those people whose epitaphs were upon the walls of the: chapel and more particularly to one whom they looked back to as having devoted himself more en- tirely to the children, and for a longer time than anyone else—Dr. Carpenter. (Applause.) There were others too —their friend Mr. Filcher. (Applause.) How he would have been gladdened at the eight. All should be glad- dened,and hope that the beaut;ful building they entered that day would take in part among the educational in- stitutions of Warrington. He must not forget to give in their name and his own their grateful thanks to Mr. Owen, the architect, for the noble building he had raised. There was the old saying " A thing nf beauty is a ;joy for ever," and he thought that building would take its place among the beautiful buildings ha Warrington. .(Applause.) He was thank- ful to hear that in its erection no accident whatever haci happened and that all had gone smoothly. He would also thank the iuilder for the effort he had made in the past few weeks to be ready in time for the opening cere- mony. 'Money matters he was loth to mention there,but he might say that as nearly as possible they had opened the building free from debt. There would be a certain amount of expense with regard to furnishing and if any members of the congregation or friends would like to eave something behind they would be glad to receive it. He was sure that in the name of the congregation he could bid everybody a hearty welcome and extend thanks to those friends who had come from a distance to jointhem. (Apalause). Mr. THOMAS Brecreaet said he had been requested, he presumed; as one of the oldest members of the congrega- donl to move a vote of thanks to Mrs. Shipman, to the archlect and builder, and to the many others who had gives them their kindly help, and come to rejoice with them that day. (Applause.) It was a red-letter day iu the history of Caircestreet chapel,and its history had not been a mean one. He could look back on its history over SO years and could mention the good men who had occupied their pulpit and striven to make the life of Warrington sweeter and better; he looked back with a feeling of thankfulness and reverence for their memory. (Hear.hear.) They had done something for Warrington, which was not strong in architectural beauties, in erect- iug a building which would.as Mr. Long had said.be " a thing of beauty and a joy for ever" and a pleasure to all who had taken part in its erection. He never passed the Town ,Hall gates without thinking that a ann of Cairo-at. had placed them there. (Applause.) After referringin complimentary terms to the work of Mr. W. ' Owen ,(arehitect), and Mr. Collin (the builder) be said he was proud to think that their congregation had always taken its fair share in the public life of Warrington. That day was not an exception. It had always had men able and willing to take their full share of public duties, and had done it in a way that had called forth the com- mendation of their fellow men. (Applause.) With the preepects before them they should look for more. With the aid -ofthat excellent 'building the training in their Sunday school would be better. It had been hieh before ctbruettn; otwilnythitt tyhdehe would the lhdmb eore ablep teachersletaos pleasure uatl nd have hder satisfactionwoirn km thatoreitnoeeffitaili concerned. (Applause.) Their friend Mr. Filcher would have rejoiced in the day. He had longed for it. They rejoiced also to think that what they had desired they ha.d.accomplished. He was delighted to see ao many ministers present, including Mr. Freeston. (Applause.) Councrllor Mozels said it gave him great pleasure that i day to be n the fortunate position as seconder of the resolution. As they saw for themselves, the work was now over, and the ,committee was very glad to be is a position to turn over the buildings for their further use and occupation. (Applause.) He hoped the work they had put in the building would be a long and lasting benefit to Warrington as a whole. (Applause.) The motion was then carried unanimously. Mr.W. Owstt responded, and after acknowledging the compliments he had received, said he hoped the build- ing and its rooms would answer their purpose even better than they anticipated. Mr!. SHIPMAN also responded, and expressed her plea- sure in coming to Warrington, and her willingness to come on future occasions. At five o'ciock tea was -partaken cf by's large number of those present.

THE EVEkING MEETING.—INTERESTING ADDRESSES. A'well attended public meeting was held in the even- ing in the large seheolroom.under the presidency of Mr. F. Monks, J. P., C.C. A number of beautiful planta had been placed around the platform, and presented a pleas- ing appearance. On the ola.tferm. In addition to the chairman, there were the Rev. Broeks Heger& Rev. W. H. Drummond, 8.A.., Rev, F. K. Freeston, Rev. H. S. Taylor, M.A., Messrs. Wnlter 'H. Travers. W. Long. or J.nßool:b.., saotantn.ednfdoJ:. ninf Iceeoruiwygerhatemo nree. ma eitLeirvn ecorifua I dtlihenetet eir, no o ff r oamP,o sin erY. W. gr also one from tte. Rev. sohnTonite, of own ycengffaati co nh.d racnhu. The Rev. W. H. Drummond said it was a great regret to him that they would not have the pleasure of listening to Mr. Yonge's voice that night. The CIikIRYLN said it had been very truly said that afternoon that that wait • red letter day in the history of their congregation. He wac one of those who was old enough to remember when that congregation was much smaller than it was that day. Ile whaled the young to remember that nothwithatanding small things they mtist never lose heart. (Applause.) Ile was travelling with a worthy townsman not very long ago, and that gentle- man put to him the question, what was Unitarianism P He (Mr. Monks) confessed that for the moment he could not give him an answer satiafactfi.y to his own mind. He told him what it was not, but he could not tell him what it was. However, on refection, for himself, he should define it to be a firm belief in religion with a spirituel basis. If be had to define his own position he should say that he was a Unitarian quaker. He did not believe in the creeds and doctrines taught by their orthodox friends, but he did believe in what the quaker' called inspiration. One of the con- dition e of Unitarian life was held to he perfect religious liberty,and their forefathers fought for it two hundred years ago.Tbey reverenced them for it. They looked back on the roany men who had worked at that charch and school with deep reverence and affection. He was quite satisfied that the result of their life had been on the spiritual hole to which he had referred. With one of them he had had a great deal to do, and his always felt thankful that he knew h;m, and also that he had known two or three others connected with that congregation. (Applause.) fie had never formed the opinion that Unitarianism would build up large congregations such as the orthodox bodies. No society where men of neces- city thought for themselves and as • result of so doing formed an ideal which they strove to embody in the actual life, would have such large numbers as flocked together in the .Orthodox churches. Therefore they must not be surprised if in the course of time they did not prosper as some of them would wish. But he hoped that the building they had dedicated that day would produce such resultaas that old schoolroom had done, and the school that was carried on in the chapel in his earlier days, and also as their congregations had pro- duced in that town for over two hundred years. (Ap-

plause.) If it did nothing more than produce a few such men as many of them could name, he thought that the money which had been spent and the efforts they had put forth would be amply repaid. (Applause.) The building up of character was not a work of a day. Many of them knew, and he might say that every body, including the orthod-x body, would willingly admit that the Quakers and Unitarians had produced in proportion to their numbers, a much larger number of public spirited, high-toned men than any ether two sects they could name. If that was so.and everybody admitted it, they might depend upon it that the success,the strength, was in the building up of character on the basis he had referred to. It was a fine thing to provide a home for those who felt they could worrhip with them without being creed-bound. They had been broadening the churches, and Unitarianism as a spiritual power and force had taken possession of the orthodox churches and was bringing them up to their level, and they were all the better for it. He remembered as a boy, that the orthodox bodies would not admit a. Unitarian on the Bible Society's platform and he could speak of many instances where Unitarians were made to feel the isola- tion of their position and made to suffer for their belief in the form of faith they professed. For himself, it did not matter very much whether a man called the Infinite a force or regarded it as God, so long as he recognised the right of every man to choose his own form of belief, which he felt best suited to his needs. In conclusion, he said he trusted that the teachers and young people who had to carry on the work after many of them had gone, would do so in the same spirit as their predecessors, and recog- nise the liberty of each to think and act for himself as had been the case there for many years. It had always been a source of pain to him when he thought of the disruption that took place there many years ago. He ventured to say that if there had been a little more charity allowed for differences of opinion, that disrup- tion would never have happened, and they at Cairo-st, would have been all the stronger during the last thirty years. It was a matter for rejoicing to many of them that in these latter years they had come together in per- fect harmony and worked in harmouy and concord, and he hoped that would continue with the congregation for many years to come. (Applause.) Dr. EIERFORD said that meeting and that coming back to Warrington after so many years of absence was to him more than any of them could quite understand. The two men who had been most helpfu to him during the 45 years of his ministry, were Charles Madge and Philip Carpenter. (Applause.) He first made the acquaint- ance of Philip Carpenter when he (Dr. Herford) was a growing lad of seventeen. Philip L:irpenter got hold of his young heart and was one of the beet friends he had during the year he was preparing to go to college. when he (the speaker) was in college, Philip Carpenter came to Warrington, and he spent a part of every vacation with him at Warrington. Whenever he did come to visit Philip Carpenter at Warrington he was always sure that he would be set to work, and kept at it until nearly ten o'clock at night. (Laughter.) Dr. Herford related many of his experiences with Philip Carpenter at Warrington in his philanthropic and educational work. Referring to the Rev. Richard Pilcher, Dr. Herford said he knew him when they both worked at business together in Manchester. They both decided to enter the ministry, but Mr. Pitcher was a dozen years later than he (Dr. ' Herford) was in entering college. Both of them worked hard as they bad to work their passage. (Laughter.) He eas glad to see the old school and chapel at Cairc- street, prospering. Although he had not been in War- rington for many years, yet to come and see the new work they were opening told him of the noble spirit that had been in them during those years, and it made them , stronger that day than they had ever been. He wished I them God-speed in everything they were going to do in those beautiful rooms that they had dedicated to the new service. (Applause.) Mr. Wit Tint MATERS said as one who had had the honour of presiding at the superintendent's desk of that Sunday school for a term of something like five years he felt that he could venture without apology to say a few words of felicitation on that interesting occasion. He rejoiced with them in the erection of those new build- ings. As one who had left the school and congregation he could not do better than wish that others would carry ,away with them pleasant and helpful memories as he had done. It must he with honourable pride that those who had worked for that school extension realised at last that it was an accomplished fact, and that must be especially so to the chairman. It must also be very gratifying and encouraging to the minister, for although Mr. Drummond would be one of the first to recognise in that extension the fruition of the geed sown by his pre- decessors, yet had it not been for the life and vigour infused by Mr. Drummond and the confidence he had inspired such a harvest could not have been garnered as was the case that day. It was his (Mr. Travers's) priv- ilege to be a scholar and worker in that Sunday school for 14 or /5 years, 9 ef which were covered by the minis- try of that highly respected and revered preacher, Richard Pitcher. (Applause.) The Rev. F. K. FaISSTON said nothing could be more interesting and enjoyable than that historic occasion when they met to mingle reminiscences with anticipa- tions for the future. When they met to God-speed the new building on its way, they must not look down with disdain upon its forerunner, but think of it as a build- ing round which had clustered many associations and many memories. He had been thinking of the great things which had happened in that room, the school ser- vices whiCh had beers practised over, and the discus-. sions about the anniversaries. He realised afresh the immense value of their Sunday schools. They knew there were times when Sunday schools were not prosper- ing when people a ould tell them that Sunday schools which did their work in the past had not now the same work to do. His firm conviction was that Sunday solead work was never more important or more urgent than at the present moment. (Applause.) What would Warrington have been without Cairo-st Sunday school? Philip Carpenter did great things for the chapel but greater things for the school. He was remembered more in the school. It was the school that fed the church. He could not help but feel when they were invited to consider carefully the new project for their national education, and when one item of that project was a sug- gestion to introduce into the national schools those sec- tarian beliefs which were best kept out of it—(hear, hear)—that the need for Sunday school work was urgent and important. In their Sunday school they imparted religious instruction and spiritual religious in- duenee wholly apart from those dividing creeds and dogmas which so often, instead of furthering the Christ-like spirit seemed on the other hand to rend it asunder and draw them apart one from another, He felt, therefore, that at the same time as they were open- ing up a new'chapter in the history of their grand old Vilarrineton school, they were entering upon a period in their edunational history when the duty and uss of the despised Sunday school would be more fully recognised. (applause.) Ile prayed that all the teachers in that school aud all those who grew up within its walls, whether in the old or new, might have the privi- lege of helping on that religious reformation taken in the children which had to be brought about, and that ' God's blessing might rest upon their work. (Applause.) The Rev. H. 6. TiervEß (president of the Manchester District Sunday School Association) said they knew that Sunday schools had been carried on under the most dis- advantageous circumstances. He believed no Christian church met its highest development unless it paid atten- tion to the young. Be believed they were d -)ing well by finding a pleasant place like they were doing at Caho- ot., for it would have an influence on the children, but roots would depend on the smiles of the teachers. It seemed to him the noblest work in which men and wo- men could possibly engage. It was most Christlike, the taking of the children in a loving spirit and endeavour- ing to quicken in them the most precious spirit—the re- ligious spirit. (Applause.) The Rev. W. H. Direstwcreo said it was impossible for • minister of a congregation that had taken such a step as Cairo-st. not to have some feeling of pride in his heart. It was a work that was in the widest and truest sense a new work. It had been work which many people had thought about, and one to which many people had given of their means. They had had their princely givers amongst them,but they had also had their widows' mites for which they were thankful no less. It showed that there was a strong expression and strong religious feel- ing in the matter. Two of their great workers had been singled nut.but they must not forget to pay a warm tri- bute to the memory of the other workers. Some of their names had been inscribed on the tablet in the chapel. He was thankful to believe that they had their self- sacrificing workers to-day. (Applause.) The longer he was in the ministry and the closer he came in con- tact with Sunday school work,the more he honoured the men and women who were doing that work. (Applause.) The buildings had been built and dedicated for religious uses. That did not mean that they must take a narrow and restricted view of things. They were going to teach religion there. They were going to teach the children about Jesus Chriet.and to try and impress them with the dignity and great responsibility of life. They would have their distinctly educational agencies and their re- creative clanes.their times for recreation, and their par- ties. Religion,God. Christ, and love, these were to be the objects of their efforts, and might God grant that some of them would be remembered with the same affection as had bean the lot of many workers In the past. (Applause.)

- Mr. !lull: (senior inmerintendent of the school) pro- posed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and to the visi- tors who had spoken. Referring to Mr. Monks, he said he was their "grand old man." and they were all very proud of him. They had heard a great deal about Sun- day schools, hut they must not lose sight of the fact the the buildings were not only for Sunday school work but also for concregational purposes. Mr. T. C. EIOLI INGWORTH (secretary), having alit: spoken, the Chairman and the Rev. Dr. Herford res- ponled, and the meeting concluded with the pronounc- ing of the Benediction.

Dr. Biroorte HERPORD preached in the chapel both morning *nu evening on Sunday, the Rev. W. 11. Drum- rucnd conducting the preliminary portion of the services. In the muming Mr. Rerford preached on " Companion- ship in religious u‘,.;rship." basing his remarks on Malachi ,16 ; "They that feared the Lord spoke often one to another," In the evening, to & large congregation, he preached an impressive sermon on "Supplying other people's ioek of service,' taking tor his text Philippians ii, 30,

div.head: WARRINGTON AGENT AND HIS COMMISSION.
div.p: A WARRINGTON AGENT AND HIS COMMISSION.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday morning,before his Honour Judge Wynne Pfoulkes, a case was heard in which Messrs. John Pendlebury and Company, Winwick-street, Warrington, claimed .£lO Os. 9d. from Thomas Ellison, 25, Legh- street, Warrington,insurance and commission agent, who made a counter-claim of £9 2s. 6d. for commis- sion on orders received.—Mr. A. Browne repre- sented the plaintiffs, and Mr. P. Davies defended. —ln stating the case, Mr. Browne pointed out that the claim was for money lent to the defendant, amounting to .£9 28. 6d., and the rest of the account was for coal supplied and is. overpaid on commis- sion. The plaintiffs were furniture dealers and they employed the defendant in 1892 to collect from certain customers on commission. They handed him a book which had been formerly collected by Mr. Pickup and also another one formerly in the possession of Mr.lleywood. The arrangement with the defendant was that he should have 10 per cent commission on monies received. For the first few weeks after he started, the amount of commission was very small, and therefore at defendant's re- quest, Mr. Pendlebury advanced him 10s. each week for a number of weeks and the defendant agreed to repay it at 28. 6d. per week when he was doing better. The sum lent to the defendant was £9 10s., and since the defendant had left Mr. Pendlebury's employ he had paid three separate sums of 2s. ed. each. Mr. Pendle- bury ceased to employ the defendant when he found that he was selling furniture on his own account. The result was that Mr. Pendlebury got the worst debts and the defendant supplied the best customers. The de- fendant Old the plaintiff that he was going to open a shop on his own account, and Mr. Pendlebury told him that it was impossible for him to serve two masters and that he should not have him in his employ any longer. The plaintiff never heard of the counter-claim until three weeks after he had entered his claim against the defendant. It was a counter-claim for commission on orders received, but the defendant knew very well that he was only paid commission on 'money he collected. During the four years the defendant was in the plain- tiff's employ he never made a claim for commission on orders received. It would be unreasonable to expect it when the goods were chiefly supplied on the hire-pur- chase system. None of the other agents in the employ of the plaintiff received commission on orders.

Frederick Pendlebury,trading as John Pendlebury and Company, and carrying on business as furniture and coal dealers, corroborated Mr. Browne's statement—!n cross-examination witness said he did not dispute that the defendant h.d got the orders for which he claimed commission, but they never paid their agents on the orders they received bat en the money they collected for them. Many of the orders had turned out to be bad debts He did not know that the defendant's wage. had only averaged 5. a week.—Benry Cottier, in the employ of Messrs. Pendlebury and Company, spoke to having re- ceived several amounts from the defendant towaras the reduction of the debt on the money owing for money lent.

Mr. Davies, for the defence, said the terms on which the defendant was engaged were that he was to receive ten per cent on isles affected. Not a word was said about commission on money collected. The defendant had got orders for goods amounting to £9l 3s. 11d., and he was entitled to the commission he had claimed.

His Honour said there had been no objection to the plaintiff's claim, and there must be judgment for the plaintiff as far as the claim was concerned. The evid- ence must be confined to the counter-claim.

Thomas Ellison, 25, Legh-street, said Mr. Pendlebury agreed to pay him ten per cent. Oh all orders secured, but that be would pay him the -rommissi nas he col- lected the money for the goods supplied. The counter- claim was for commission on orders he had obtained,but for which he had not collected the money. It was impossible for him to do so. when he was not in the employ of the plaintiff.—ln cross-examination, witness admitted that he had received 10 per cent. commission on money he had collected from Pickup's and Heywood's books, the orders for which he had not obtained.
His Honour said he must give judgment for the plain- tiff on the claim and counter-claim. The pla ntiff had not proved that the COMMillBiol2 was te be paid on all orders received.
