WHAT I HAVE SEEN I HAVE SEEN.

"We saw her gradually faling away under that try- ing cough to almost a skeleton." So writes a fath r about his little child. You ctai almost imagine what had happened in that household. Sometimes it all begins with bronchitis, again it is whooping cough, and frequently an ordinary cold starts baby fading away to almost a skeleton. In Mr. Gordon's case it happened, to quote his own language, in this way .

'About a year ago, our little daughter Violet, now three and a half years old, had a severe attack of whoop- ing cough. Prior to that time, she had been one of the brightest, healthiest babies in the world. She had no difficulty cutting her teeth, and we were always very much surprised ourselves to think that she should keep so well. When the whooping cough came on,we thought that her vitality would carry her through nicel7,and we did not worry until we noticed that the coughing was becoming chronic, and baby was growing thin under the strain. We then became very nervous over her, for we saw he gradually fading away under that trying cough to almost a skeletor. She lost her appetite, grew pale and weak, and in September we had almost given up hopes of raising her. She was listless, her eyes were dull ; in fact, she was almost lifeless, except for that cough, cough. cough. A friend advised us early in September to try Scott's Emulsion. This friend was so earnest, that we decided to try it, and I can now say that our little girl owes her life to it. Scott's Emulsion eased her coughing at once, loosened the phlegm n her little throat, restored her appetite, and soon we • began to see her picking up in flesh and strength. In less than a month she was a different child, and appeared really like her old self again. Scott's Emulsion absolutely cured her cough, made her fat, gave her a rosy colour, and made her strong and robust in every way. She is now all animation, and one of the healthiest children you have ever seen,—Yours faithfully (signed) SAML. GORDON, 22, Colehill Road, Munster Road, Fulham, S.W.,January 30th, 1896.

You will notice that Scott's Emulsion did more than stop the child's coughing. It" made her fat, gave her a rosy colour, and made her strong and robust in every way." This would have been the effect if the little girl had merely been thin, pale and weak. It is always so with children that do not thrive. Scott's Emulsion nourishes them and gives them strength when it almost seems impossible to raise them.
You can distinguish the genuine Scett'a Emulsion by the trade-mark of a fisherman holding a big fish on his back. It is on the wrapper of every genuine bottle. (18)

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
FRIDAY.

The House afterwards went into committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, and on the vote for £29,400 for the Colonial Services Sir W. Harcourt said that it was nearly three months since there had been any discussion in the House on South African Affairs. The right hon. gentleman proceeded to contend that the Jameson ra;d had been conducted by persons who were the principal and responsible directors of the Company ; that Dr. Jameson was but a subordinate agent in the matter; and that it was consequently with the direc- tors of the Company that they would have to deal. He entered into an analysis of the cipher messages—the " low morality and vulgar slang," of which were, he said,revolting to any high-minded man, and presented a " sordid,squalid picture of stockbroking imperialism."— and argued that British honour had been sullied by the acts of Mr. Rhodes and his associates. He did not raise the question for the present as to whether the Chartered Company was to continue to exist. But, he asked in conclusion,were they justified in continuing the Com- pany in the hands of those who had so grossly misused and abused their power? Mr. CRAMBERLA.IN, who at once rose to reply, said re- cent events in South Africa had reopened the whole of the great South African question. Sir W. Harcourt had devoted the greater part of his speech to only one phase of that question, the position created for us by Ithe inroad into the Transvaal, and upon which light had been thrown by the cipher telegrams. There was, however, a very much wider question, and that was the policy of the Government as a whole with regard to South Africa. There were two main objects which any British Government must have in view in regard to that country. The first was the preservation of our position as the paramount State. The second object was to bring about a better state of union and cencord be- tween the two great races which now inhabited that country. He expressed the opinion that Mr. Rhodos did all he could to stop Dr. Jameson's invasion of the Trans- veal, and said he hold the view that the presence of Mr. Rhodes in South Africa was absolutely :necessary for the development and prosperity of the Company. He an- nounced that the Government had decided that aa in- quiry into the whole of the proceedings of the Chartered Company should be made by • Joint Committee of both Houses of Parliament. The debate was adjourned.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday Mr. J. Mosum asked whether there was any truth in the rumour that Indian troops were to be sent to Suakim ; whether, i• it were true, a motion would be submitted to the House in connection with the subject; and by whom the ex- pense would be borne. Lord G. Hamilton replied that the Government had decided to send certain Indian troops to replace the Egyptian garrison at Suakim,which, with the exception of one battalion, would be moved across to the Nile Valley. The appointment of the ex- pense between the Indian Government and the Govern- ment at home was still under consideration. The debate on Mr. Asquith's amendment to the mltion for the second reading of the Education Bill was resumed by Mr. John Ellis. Among the subsequent speakers were Sir E. Clarke, Mr. ?duodena, and Mr. Jebb. The de- bate was again adjourned.

In the House of Lords, Viscount Halifax moved the second reading of a bill to prevent persons who have been respondents in the Divorce Court from being mar- ried in churches or chapels of the Church of England. The fact that persons who had been convicted of mis- conduct in the Divorce Court could, if they desired to get marrie4 a second time,have the ceremony performed in a building belonging :o the Church was felt as a serious grievance by the clergy. Lord SALISBURY gave a qualified approval to the bill, and after some observe- tons hp Lords KIMBRFILBY and GRIBTHORPIC it was read a second time. The Select Committee on the Companies Acts was appointed.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Is the House of Comm6ns on Tuesday Sir M. Warr% RIDLRY, stated, in answer to a question put by Dr. Clark, that he had received a communication from the Lord Chief Justice in regard to the case of Mrs. May- brick, to which he had given his most anxious considers- tip:lr The responsibility for the decision he came to was his own, and he had no intention of appointing a Commission of inquiry. Questioned by Mr. Labouchere as to the speech made by Mr. Rhodes at Gwelo on Friday last, and the position Mr. Rhodes at present occupied, Mr. CumeeperoarN said he had seen a telegraphic report of the speech. Pend- ing the arrival in the field of Sir F. Carrington, Sir R. Martin would have supreme command of the forces. Mr. Rhodes was, as any other colonist might be.holding the township of Gwelo against the enemy at the head of a body of colonists like himself. Asked by Mr. Labou- chere whether Mr. Rhodes adhered to his statement that he had no knowledge of DrJaineson's raid before it took place,and as to how the letter from Johannesburg to Dr. Jameson came to be printed by the " Times" on the day the frontier WAR crocsed. Mr. Chamberlain said he had had no communication with Mr. Rendes since he left England. As the other points in the question touched on matters which were the subject of injuiry in a court of law, he must decline to answer them. Mr. Chamberlain, in reply to Sir E. A. Bartlett. said he was sorry he had rece ved no communication from the Boer Government with reference to the sentences passed on the Reform leaders at Pretoria. In answer to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. CURZON said the troops to be et. tit from India would be employed for the defence of Suakim and the surrounding district, No agreement had been entered into between the Govern- ment and the Italian Government in respect of military action in the Snudan. The troops from India would con- sist of about 50 British and 60 native officers, and from 2,000 to 2,500 men. By 279 votes to 153 the twelve o'clock rule was sus- pended, and the debate on Mr. Asquith's amendment to the motion for the second reading of the E iucatinn Bill was resumed by Colonel Mellor. Mr. Acland followed, and he was succeeded by Sir J. Fergusson. Mr. Balfour wound up the debate from the Ministerial side. Mr. C. Shaw essayed to move the adjournment of the debate, but was prevented from speaking by cries of " Divide." Mr. BALFOUR moved the closure, which WAR carried by 379 votes to 198. The motion for the second reading was carried by 423 votes to 156, a majoriey of 267. The bill was then read a second time, and the House adjourned.

div.head: WEST AUSTRALIAN GOLD SHARES.
div.p: WEST AUSTRALIAN GOLD SHARES.

Until lately, it has been a question whether the Gold Mines of West Australia hold good at depth ; but now itr has been proved that they are well defined lodes in fig.. sure veins and only require to be properly developed' and worked to pay handsome dividends on the money invested. The latest reports from the Manager of the Guelph Gold Mines, Limited, Coolgardie, whose property is on the Royal Sovereign line of reef, about 400 yard', north of the Royal Sovereign Mine, are most satisfac,- tory, and state that " all the men at present employed on the mines are first-class miners ; hence the work pro- gresses satisfactorily. No. 1 inclined shaft has been sunk to a depth of 701 t. on a splendid reef.both walls of which are well defined. Samples taken from different parts of the reef give from Ito s)z. of gold to the ton." Several shafts have been sunk along the reefs, the ore from which has produced payable gold in each instance, and ths samples of the gold reef taken from the main shaft; give assays of from Ito 5 oz.s. of gold per ton. This is. it is thought, likely to prove one of the richest Gold Mines in %Vest Australia.and there are signs that Guelph Gold Mine Shares will soon become a prominent feature iL. the %Vest Australian market. Their present price is only ss. per Sbare,fully paid,and they look very cheap.

A GREAT wEsr AUSTRALIAN PARENT COMPANY. There are signs of an impending r.ninibg boom in West Australia, now that some of the biggest financiers are extensively interested in West Australian properties. The Shares of the West Australian Gold Properties De-. velopment Company, Limited, now that large profits and good dividends are assured, are rising rapidly ick price on the London Stock Exchange; their present price—£2 53. per Share fully paid up—leaves room for a considerable advance. These securities should be- cheap at a much higher quotation, for it is expected that good dividends will soon be announced. The Com- pany has secured the right to prospect for gold and all other minerals, and to purchase no less an area than 76,000 acres,freehold in one of the best known and most important parts of West Australia, and is also interested in many of the most valuable g-ld properties in that Colony, one of which has in iti first crushing, given ore yielding Soz. of gold to the ton. The acquisitions of the Company are ruching a magnitude which was not in the first instance anticipated, and the concern is now getting in a position to reap the advantages and profits arising from the forming of subsidiary Companies to work portions of its large estates. It is also getting in- to its hands other highly valuable properties, and pro- mises to become one of the grAtest parent organisa- tions in West Australia.

div.head: CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON
div.p: CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON
WATCH REPAIRER.
A WITNESS TURNED OUT OF COURT.

On Thursday week, at the Warrington County Court, before his Honour Judg• Wynne Ff ulkes, Thomas Jack snn beer-house keerer, Dial-strea, Warrington, claimed £8 75., or the return of the watch or its value £7 7s. and £1 damages for detention, from William Dodwell, man- ager of the Liverpool Watch Repairing Company, Winwick-street, Warrington. Mr. Percy Davies, solici- tor, ranresented the plaintiff. Mr. Davies said the plaintiff's watch was repaired by the defendant last year. but as it again got out of order he took it once more to the plaintiff on the 22nd of January fast to be put right. A few days afterwards he called for it, and the defendant told him that he had lost it. He said he took the watch with him to the Waggon and Horses pub- lic-house the same night be received it, and whilst there he waerobbed of it by some women. He had put the matter in the hands of the police and would very likely be able to get it back. The plaintiff, on enquiry at the Police Station, found that the defendant had reported the loss of a watch, but he (Mr. Davies) woeld be able to bring witnesses before his Honour who would prove that the watch was seen on the defendant's premises some days after he had stated that it was lost. Mr. Thomas Jackson the plaintiff, said the watch was a gold faced one for which he paid £7 7s. in 1875 to Mr. Harris. of Manchester.—Mary Jackson, daughter of the plaintiff, deposed that she called at the defendant's shop a few days after the defendant had told her father, that he had lost the watch. The defendant was not in, but his assistant was there, and elle saw him with the watch in his hand.—The assistant alluded to, stood up in court, and shouted' It is a lie."—Mr. Davies• said he objected to the witness being interrupted in that manner.—His Honour : Turn that man out of Court.—The defendant: He is my witness.—His Honour : The man must be turned out of Court.—The man was thereupon removed by a bailiff. Witness, continuing her evidence, said the defendant's assistant knew it was her father's watch. He said it was not repaired yet_ —Sarah Ann Wright corroborated the last witness's statement as to seeing the watch in the defendant's shop when she went in company with her.—The defendant said he did not know where he lost the watch. He went to the Waggon and Horses public-house with the watch in his pocket, and had something to drink. He got ab the back of Dial-street.and he asked a policeman to shoe him the way to Rewsey where he lived. He did not know how he lost the watch from his pocket.—Mr. Davies : You were drunk then P—Defendant : suppose I was.—His Honour said the defendant's own statement was quite enough to make him liable for the watch.—Defendant said the case was a disgraceful affair.—Mr. Davies : Very disgraceful. (Laughter.)— William Henry Dodwell said he was a son ot the defend- ant. It was untrue that he showed the defendant's daughter her father's watch. He never saw it on the day in question. He did not think the watch was worth more than 451. when new.—ln cross-examination wit-, ness said he was sure he was the son of the defendant. He had been at the Wiawick-street shop about fourteen months. He knew that there had been a robbery com- mitted by one of toe managers of the shop. The watch might have cost £7 7s. about 27 years age.—His Honour said he would give a verdict for the plaintiff for £5 and one shilling for detention or the watch to he returned within a week.—Defendant : If the watch is recovered after I have paid the money what must I do.—His Honour: Keep the watch. (Laughter.)

div.p: DIE EXA_MINEIi.
SATURDAY, MAY 16th, 1896.

A FEW months ago Mr. CHAm- A Weak Policy. BERLAIN won great praise from all parties in the country—with the exception, perhaps, of the extreMe Jingo sec- tion of his own party—for the sensible and vigor- ous action he took with respect to the JAMESON raid. He denounced that raid as a lawless and utterly unjustifiable invasion of a friendly coun- try, and after the defeat and capture of the inva- ders he brought JAMESON and his principal officers to England to be tried for a serious international offence. Since then the situation has greatly

changed. It was alleged at that time that JAME- SON only was to blame for the invasion of the Transvaal, and that a great deal was to be said in extenuation of any offence that he might have committed. It was suggested that he had set his troops in motion upon a sudden impulse after reading an appeal for help from Johannesburg,and that his motives were, therefore, purely humani- tarian. This fine plea, although sceptically re- ceived by most people, • could not he refuted till the famous cypher telegrams were published a week or two ago. It was then seen that the invasion was not due to any sudden impulse. It was seen that it was part of a scheme which had, to use the forcible language of Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, been "long devised, secretly and fraudulently hatched by a stock-job- bing syndicate." At the head of that syndicate was Mr. RHODES, the Prime Minister of Cape Colony, and managing director of the South African Company whose extensive charter was obtained from Lord SALISBURY'S previous govern- ment. The cypher telegrams do not make the , case against Dr. JAMESON any worse than it was before; on the other hand, they show that he was , merely a subordinate in a plot in which Mr. RHODES and the Chartered Company were princi- pals.., It was naturally thought, therefore, that the Government which had ordered the prosecu- tion of Dr. JAMESON would feel bound to extend the scope of the inquiry so as to include the 'actions of Mr. RHODES and the Chartered Com- pany generally. But this is just what the Government have not done. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN—Who seems to be in great danger of spoiling the fine reputation he:gained at the commencement of the year—when dealing with the subject in the House of Commons took up a position which he will probably find before many weeks are over is utterly untenable. He did not take the bold and honest course of saying that all the parties against whom there was a pri2na-facie. case should be brought to an open and impartial trial; nor did he say, on the other hand, that the whole of the recent events in South Africa would be ignored by Her Majesty's Government and that the trial of Dr. JAMESON and his officers would be abandoned. Instead of either of ,these courses being taken a policy which is both feeble and discreditable has been adopted. Dr. JAME- SON will be tried for his part in the raid, but Mr. Cecil RHODES is to be allowed to remain in South Africa in that position of great authority which the managing directorship of the Chartered Com- pany of necessity gives him. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN mentioned two reasons which influenced the Government in deciding as they have done, but neither ot these reasons will bear much looking at. One is that Mr. RHODES presence in South Africa is essential to the development of the newly - acquired territory. This it will be seen, is neither . more nor less than a gratuitous libel on the administrative talent at the command of the British Govern- ment. A nation which has founded and devel- oped the colonies of America and Australasia, which governs the two hnndred odd millions of India, and which has within the last few years brought order out of chaos in Egypt, is surely net so suddenly deprived of administrative skill that it is completely dependent upon a financier of Mr. CECIL RHODES' type to control a territory thinly inhabited by Kaffirs and Zulus. The other reason is, that the taking over of the country now in the hands of the Chartered Company would entail considerable expense upon the Imperial Exchequer, but this pretext loses all its f ,rce when it is consilercal that it is made by a Governmeflt. which is handing two millions a year over to the landlerds and other large sums to the voluntary schools. Behind all these sham reasons there is the real' reason that the Chartered Company and Mr RHODES are backed by financial and social influ- ences which have immense weight with this Tory Government. When other governments or legis- latures—those, of France or America for example —allow themselves to be controlled by influences of this sort, they are roundly accused of political corruption. A few weeks ago an influential journal suggested that we might be on the eve of revela- tions in this country similar to those which were made in France in connection with the Panama scandal, and it may at once be said that the Government's refusal of a full and rigorous in- quiry into recent, events in South Africa has certainly not helped to remove suspicions of that kind.

div.p: THE EXAMINER SATUR PA Y, MAY 16 1896.

IT has been said that Mr. CHAPLIN Landlords' the President of the Board of Legislation. Trade who has charge in Parlia- ment of the Land Rating Bill, will benefit to the extent of £7OO a year, by the passing of the Bill. It is further said that the present Cabinet, which, it is needless to say, is a Cabinet of land- owners, will when combined benefit to the extent of £74,000 a year from the Bill. Yet, the Tories are constantly accusing the Liberals of class legis- lation. But whatever else may be said,no Liberal Government has ever promoted a Bill for putting £74,000 a year into their own pockets. Of course Mr. CHAPLIN hotly denies that he will benefit personally from the Bill. He argues that it is his tenants who will benefit. It is said, however, that Mr. CHAPLIN has himself pointed out in speeches made by him before this Bill was inteoduced, that landlords always ultimately receive the benefit from a relief of rates. That is, of course, the conclusion to which everyone who studies the question without personal or political bias must come. Some tenants, and especially those who have leases, may benefit for a few years from a reduction of rates, but in the end all the, advantage is secured by the landowner through the annual rent. There are probably numerous tenants who will not benefit for even a single year from the Rating Bill. During the last few years. of depression they have had their rents remitted to the extent of five, ten, or fifteen per cent., but when the next rent day comes round how easy it will be for the landlord or his agent to take into account the relief of rates in fixing the amount of the remission. It is just possible in fact, that in some cases the rent remission may be lessened by a larger sum than the farmers have saved in their rates, and in these cases the Rating Bill will prove anything but a blessing to the teeant. In the very letter which he has written to refute the argument that the landlords will benefit, Mr. CHAPLIN innocently destroys his own case. He , says, for instance, that "In these days of depres- sion in ninety-nine cases out of every hundred every change of tenancy is accompanied by a fall in the rent. No landlord '.even if he wished to do so, could appropriate the benefits of this bill without determining the tenancy; if he did so, he would at once incur the risk of a loss of rent infinitely greater than any bene- fit he could possibly derive from the bill." That is exactly what opponents of the Rating Bill have been saying. They say that landlords will benefit from the Bill in two ways—first, by being able to increase their rents, and, second, by being enabled to continue to exact an already ex- cessive rent. Mr. CHAPLIN'S statement confirms this latter argument. He, in effect, says that in "ninety-nine cases out of every hundred " the tenant is so over-rented that when he leaves his farm the rent has to be reduced. Well, now, in those circumstances what will be the effect of the Rating Bill ? Will the Bill not help the over- rented tenant to pay the excessive demands made upon him, and so make it less necessary for him to give up his tenancy and for the landlord to re- duce the rent? Clearly, that is the logical deduc- tion to make from Mr. CHAPLIN'S own statement. Yet Mr. CHAPLIN thinks he is refuting his oppon- ents. He is a worthy member of Lord SALISBURY'S Cabinet.

A step in the right direction was taken at the meeting of the Runcorn Guardians on Tuesday, when Mr. Woodward carried a resolution deferring the appointment of a school mistress for the work- house. Mr. Woodward fully explained his reason which was a desire to see the children of the work- house attending outside schools and competing on level terms with children more luckily reared. We agree with Mr. Woodward in believing that the lives of children confined rigidly to the surround- ings of a workhouse cannot be inspiring. Par bet- ter indeed is it that they should be allowed as much liberty as it is possible to give them, and the privilege of going outside to school dressed as other children are, should have very good results mentally and morally.

The finding of the remains of John Hough who for five weeks has been missing goes to clear up to a considerable extent another of the many river mysteries associated with Runcorn. There is some- thing pathetic in tte fact, of a father of a family leaving home to follow his usual employment on the water, then to be missing for five weeks and after- wards to be found buried in the sand at low tile. While there is not a suspicion of foul play, the question as to how the deceased got into the river can never be cleared up. Sympathetic people can only feel for a family whose trouble has been intensified by the five weeks of waiting before the fatal significance of the disappearance was verified by the finding of the body.

The hot weather of the past few days has brought into prominence the necessity of public baths for Runcorn. The need is one of old standing on which very little fresh can be said, and there seems less possibility of baths being provided now than ever there was. At the same time when the question of ways and means is the chief objection to the pro- vision of baths it may,be pointed out that the in- troductory @utlay in other towns has been more than wiped off by the patronage afforded the insti- tution by the public. The two chief reasons why baths should be provided are, firstly, to secure that cleanliness which is rightly judged to be next to godliness, and, secondly, a desire to inculcate amongst the young men in the town a knowledge of the useful art of swimming.

It was evident from the report of the meeting of the Warrington and District Association of the National Union of Teachers that the teachers o this district re no better satisfied with the Educa- tion Bill than teachers in otherpe,rts of the country. We do not know how it came about that the Rev. E. C. E. Csrleton figured so prominently at a meet- ing of teachers, but Mr. Carleton is always interest- ing when dealing with what may be called modern developnaents, as he reminds one so much of Mrs Partington contending against the waves of the Atlantic. The majority of teachers, like most other people who have studied the question, believe that education is best controlled by persons who are elected for that special purpose, but the present Government and Mr. Carleton are of a different opinion. They have evidently persuaded them- selves that a man whose"primary duty it is to look after what a well-known and useful member of a certain Town Council used to describe as pavage and sewage" is better qualified to manage the immensely important business of national educa- tion than any mere expert.

In the Ship Canal Bill as amended in the Commons committee, clauses have been inserted which should be the means of keeping the waters of the Canal near Warrington from becoming al- ost stagnant as was feared by some would be the case if the tidal openings were closed. It SI stipu- lated in the Bill that when the tide of the Mersey is on the ebb the Company shall within five boars from the time of high water, open the sluice at Walton Lock, and for twenty minutes this sluice will be raised to its tull extent before the sluices at Old Randles and other places are allowed to be opened. Thus a large volume of canal water near

Walton will be noured into the Mersey each tide, and this operation should have the effect of keeping the water fresher and cleaner. For any ' breach of this provision the Company are liable to a penalty of £5OO. Another provision stipulates that the Town Clerk of Warrington shall receive from the ompany diagrams on or about the first of each month, showing on each tide the heights to which and the periods during which the sluices at Walton and other places had been raisea and kept open. These diagrams are to be open for public inspection.

We understand that it is after all very probable that an amicable settlement will be arranged be- tween the Warrington Corporation and the L and N-W Railway Company with reference to the Borough Extension Bill, and that the Railway Company will not proceed with their opposition against the Bill in the House of Lords. The Lon- don and North Western Railway Bill which will shortly come before a committee of the House of Commons will be opposed by the Ship Canal Com- pany, the Warrington Corporation, and other parties interested. It is probable, however, that the opposition of the Warrington Corporation will be withdrawn as the Company have agreed to protect the interests of the Corporation with regard to sewers, gas and water mains, and to carry out certain improvements to the bridge over Factory lane and for the improved lighting of the lane.

RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

Sir J. T. Brunner, -Bart, M. P., has been unable to accept the invitation to present the cup and medals to the Runcorn F,..othall Club on the 10th inst. The pre- sentation will t,e made by the President, Mr. Speakman.

div.head: INTERESTING OPERATION ON A RUNCORN CUIMNEY.
div.p: INTERESTING OPERATION ON A RUNCORN CUIMNEY.

During the week the work of a steeple-jack has been scanned with something like awe by passengers up and down filiel-street,Runcorn. The workman who follows this daring o .cupation has been and is now engaged re- moving about 20 feet of a giant chimney on the promises of Messrs. Flazlehurst and Sons', soap works. The chimney has been considered unsafe, and the work is being done with the view of counteracting an ominous tendency to lean to one &de. CYCLING CLUB, RUNCORN.

The members of toe Saturday section held an inter- club run with the members of the Lostock Alkali C.C. The Lostock travellers were met at Frodsham and the two clubs proceeded to Chester which is becoming an increasingly popular resort. A portion of the club also visited Broughton near llawarden. The Wednesday section sele( ted Tarvin as the headquarters for their weekly outing and after tea a friendly game of associa- tion provided exercise and amusement for the rest of the afternoon.

POLICE INSPECTION AT RUNCORN. On Wedneslay, the Runcorn police were inspected by Sir Herbert Croft, Bart. There were on parade Super- intendent Okell, Inspector Hicks, five sergeants, and 18 constables. The inspector examined the new clothing and appointments, and afterwards the men were drilled by Inspector flicks. The inspector at the conclusion of the drill complimented the men on the smart manner in which they had turned out. The inspector also ex- amined the station premises with which he expressed himself satisfied. THE COUNTY COUNCIL SCHOLARSHIPS. On Saturday afternoon, through the kindness of the Technical Instruction Committee of the Runcorn Dis- trict Council the children attending the elementary schools in the neighbourhood desirous of competing for the scholmrships offered by the Cheshire County Council sat for examination in the Institute,Waterloo-road. The number of scholars who appeared for examination was 25, andzthe names of the successful ones will be an- nounced in due course. RUNCORN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CIIAPEL.. .

The Sunday school anniver;ary services were held in the above chapel on Sunday. The morning and evening sermons were preached by the Rev. W. E. Lead, of Widnes, whose addresses were listened to by crowded congregations. In the afternoon the Rev. C. de P. Gliddon,Wesleyan minister,Halton,delivored an able and instructive address. Daring the day's services the choir rendered special music in a manner which reflected great credit on the choir master and organist,Mr. W. Gittens. The collections amounted to £22, to which was added £l3 contribu ed by the scholars and teachers connected with the school, making the total a highly satisfactory return of £35. CHURCH CHOIR FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.

On Thunday evening in connection with the special service on Ascension Day at the Parish Church, the fol- lowing choirs joined in the rendering of the musical portion :—Parish, St. Michael's, Holy Trinity, and Wes- ton. The members assernbled in the National Schools from where they proceeded in pr )cession to the Parish Church. Amongst those who joined in the precession were the Venerable Archdeacon Woosman, Revs. W. H. Stables, H. 13. Firth, 11. 0. Moyle, W. Scholes, and A. Bartram. The solos in the service were sweetly inter- preted by Ma,ters Lane and Banner. The combined choirs numbered about 110 voices, and were conducted by M. James Littler, hon. choirmaster of the Parish Church. The preacher, the Ven. Archdeacon Woosman, founded his remarks on St. John iv. 22 to 23. RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.

The Annual General Meeting of the members of the above Club was held on Monday evening,Mr. J. I. HoPii- day having been voted to the chair. The Secretary, Mr. W. E. Hough, submitted his report for the past season %hien showed that 26 rnatchel had been played of which 15 were won, 7 lost, and 4 drawn, whilst 88 goals had been scored for and 49 against. The goals were ob- tained by :—A. Bailie 22, W. Peacock 20, W. Walker 18, S. Walker 8, C. Burrows 5, H. Pye 5, W. Bloor 3, F. Littler 3, J. K. Jones 2, and Paton and Carter 1 each. The team it will be remembered reached the semi-final stage of the Cup Competition, having defeated Penketh by 4 goals to 2, Warrington St. Mary's by 5 to 1 and Budworth by 6-0, but their hopes were shattered b Barnton Rovers who so decisively routed them at North- with on 7th March. The Treasurer, Mr. Hugh MeLeed, produced the balance sheet from which it appeared the I income had amounted to £36 149. 4-1., but the expendi- ture had been very heavy having amounting to £34 15s. 101, leaving a balance in hand of £1 16s. M. The auditors, Messrs. Gleave and F. Burrows, reported they had examined the books and all the entries m ide therein were correct, duly vouched, and perfectly satisfactory. The reports were unanimously received and adopted. The election of officers for the season 1896.7 was next proceeded with, the secretary and treasurer having inti- mated that it was their intention not to seek re-elec- tion. Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P„ was unanimously re- elected president, and Messrs. J. I. Holliday and Charles Richards were elected to the respective offices of secre- tary and treasurer without opposition. Messrs. F. Littler and C. Morrows were appointed auditors. Voting by ballot having been t tken, the following were declared by the Chairman, to have been duly elected to constitute the Committee :—Messrs. G. D. Grounds, J. K. Jones, F. Burrows, W. E. Hough and W. Peacock. The appoint- ments of captains and vice-captains were deferred. It was resolved that the team again join the Warrington and District Amateur Association League if deemed ad- visable. It was resolved that the best thanks of the meeting be given to the several officers for their services during the season, and also to the sellers of tickets for tLe prize drawing, whose efforts had been the means of landing the Club free from debt. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedings.

div.head: RITNCO RN RURAL- DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RITNCO RN RURAL- DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Present : Mr. J. Mclntyra (chair- man), Admiral Parry, Messrs. J. Weir, T. Lewis, J. B. Chadwick, E. Aaron, T. Wright, S. Woodward, H. E. Heywoed. J. M. Williams, E. Bretherton, J. Turner, W. Darlington, C. W. Davenport, J. W. Baguley, J. Spruce. J. Brandreth, J. Lowe; Mr. Ashton (clerk),Mr.G.Ashton (deputy clerk), Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspector), ' Messrs. Swinton and Dizgle (surveyors), and Dr. Adams (medical officer of health). SUTTON WATER SUPPLY. A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the application of the Council for sanction to borrow £BOO for works of water supply for the contributory place of Sutton, and to state that before deciding upon this application the Board would direct a local enquiry at a date to be notified. The Board re- quested to be furnished with a detailed estimate of the proposed works.—'fhe Clerk was empowered ;o reply te the letter.,

div.head: HELSBY AND PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES:
div.p: HELSBY AND PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES:

Mr. Jeffs, jun., clerk to the -Helsby Parish Council wrote saying the following re. olution had been adopted "That the clerk wtite to the clerk of the District Coun- cil asking on what authority it was stated at their last meeting that the Helsby Parish Council had request?d to be appointed a parochial committee. Also to Flak what increased expenditure being a parochial committee involveJ.—The Clerk was instructed to reply. .

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL MIL. Mr. Heywood presented the report of the deputation that had attended the House of Commons Committee on the Ship Canal Bill. Mr. Heywood further added that through their action in conjunction with other bodies, particularly Helsby and Frodsham Drainage Board and those acting for the estate of the Captain Park Gate., they had secured considerable modifications of the Bill. The very limited period during which the nominal level ot the water was to be exceeded was °win' to their exertions and other matters had crept into the bill through their opposition. They had not go.. all tury wantt d and he considered their case would be very strong if they opposed the Bill in the House of Lords. He proposed that the Council give the Clerk all the necessary powers to petition against the Bill in the House of Lords.—Mr. Aaron seconded, and said that the matter was a very serious one for the Council.—The resolution was then unanimously pasied. HONOURS FOR THE CHAIRMAN._ . .

The Clerk read a letter from the County Council with regard to the Chairman of the District Council taking the oath as a magistrate.—Mr. Brandreth considered th It Mr. Mclntyre, their chairman ought to be made a pe manent justice of the peace as he . had been engaged in ooblic work for over 35 years. He proposed that the Cle lc forward a petition to the Lord Lieut. of the County sung that the name of their Chairman should be permanently placed on the commission of the peace.— Mr. Heywood seconded the resolution, and expressed an opinion that the chairmen of District Councils .all over the country should have the same honour comferred upon them.—Mr. Woodward supported the resolution which was unanimously passed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams stated in his report that there had been an epidemic of mcailes at Kingsley rising in one week from one case to 56 out of a school of 186 scholars. He re- ported the matter to two Guardians who recommended the closing of the school which had been done. A simi- lar condition was reported to be in progress at Norley and a similar course had been adopted. A considerable number of cases of measles had occurred at IVeston Point. There had been one case of scarlet fever at Pres- ton Brook,three at Sutt:Nn,three at Stockton.Heath,three at Acton Grange,and two at Daresbury. There had been one case of typhoid fever at Daresbury. One case of typhus fever had broken out in Halton-road,Halton.and four cases of typhus fever had been reported from Sea_ lane, Halton, two of which had ended fatallv.—The Council confirmed the closing of the schools at Kingsley and Norton. This concluded the business of public interest.

ALLEGED DEATH THROUGH NEGLECT AT RUNCORN.

THE HUSBAND COMPLETELY EXONERATE"). Mr.Worsley held an inquest at the Police Station, Runcorn on Friday afternoon on the body of Elizabeth Bridgewater, aged 32, wife of James Bridgewater, 99, Shaw-st , who died under some- what peculiar circumstances on Wednesday last. Ellen Oliver, 13, Egerton-et., a midwife, said she at- tended deceased six weeks ago on the 28th March, in her confinement. The child was living at present but it seemed convulsive and she did not think it would live very long. The mother made a good recovery but was in a very weak state and had no appetite. They had a great difficulty to get her to take nourishment as she was in low spirits and very much depressed. The busb tnd paid her,and was there the first three days and was very attentive to his wite and anxious to get her everything she (witness) suggested. As deceased could not take gruel he asked ner to recommend to him what to get. Beef tea, mutton and eggs were provided but deceased could not take them. Deceased was very weak and low and said '• she did not want to live:" The husband showed every kindness to her. She did not see I any dispute between the husband , ad wife. The mother I of the deceased attended the confinement and was very I kind to her. Dr. Ormsby asked if the deceased came downstairs' three days afterwards. Witness replied that she did get up three days after the confinement, but not with her consent. Matilda Withey, wile of Charles Withey, of 40, Shaw- st., said she never knew the deceased until the 24'h March, when she first began to do her washing. She remembered that deceased was confined and saw her the first day she came down, when she looked very weak. There seemed to be no want, and deceased admitted that her husband allowed her 30s. per week. Ann Healey, 9, New-it., said deceased was very weak beforo her confinement. There was plenty of food in the house and decea. ed's husband was very good to her. Deceased said " +lte would rather die than get better," and was in a very low condition and would not take any food. Mary Lockett, 96, Shaw-street, wife of Thomas Lockett, said she lived opposite to the deceased, she did not know the deceased but was asked to go acre s and see her on Tuesday. Deceased was sitting in a chair ; she offered her some food but deceased would not touch

it. Dr. Ormsby said he had known he deemed since February. He was sent for first to attend one of the children that was ill. She seemed to him then to be in a very weakly condition. He saw her on the 7:h April, when he was called to see her. She was in bed in a weak, nervous frightened state. He prescribed for her and found it was difficult to get her to take any nourish- ment. He thought that her stomach was too weak to take food. She was nursing the child herself and was not in a condition t) do so. He attended her up to the 20:h, and dining that time she made some progress. The mother of deceased was with her all the time he attended her. From the way deceased spoke to him she seemed to be unable to afford the necessaries he recommended. She did not want him to call on her,and she did not seem to take either medicine or advice. He saw the husband three times. Cu the first occasion he seemed to have had some drink, and he (witness) told him that it weuld be more creditable to him if he would spend the money in necessaries for his wife instead of drink. On the second occasion Bridgewater had had drink but was not so bad as he was the first time he (witness) met him.—The Coroner: Would it not have been a good case for the nurse ?—Witness : Yes,it would. My advice was that she required care and proper nurs- ing, and no doubt a good nurse would have saved her. Continuing, Dr. Ormsby said_he considered the woman ought not to have been left on the Wednesday !naming when she was found in the house dead. He told the husband the night before the death that he might ex- pect to find her dead any time he got back. Death was due to "pernicious ansem.ea," or loss of blood. James Bridgewater said deceased was his wife and they had been married 11 years. She had got through Previous confinements very well, but of late had been going in a" backward way." His wife would have no one in to look after her. He gave her 30s. per week to keep house and th;nking that she did not like to pay someone to stay with her out of that he left her 103. The night before she died she wanted to go home as she thought the fresh air would do her good. He thought she would not be able to travel and called in Dr. Ormsby and the doctor said she would be able to travel with someone with her but recommended that she should get stronger. The Coroner in putting the case to the jury said there was little doubt if the deceased had been properly nursed by a person who would have stood over and seen that she took her food, her life might have been saved. Deceased was mistress of her own house, was 32 years old and had had five children before and he believed she was adverse to having anyone with her. While they could not help admiring the woman for her persistency in doing for nerself as long as she could yet they must feel extremely sorry that her persistency had Cost her the sacrifice of her life. • Then came the question as to whether the husband had provided the necessaries which the state of his wife required. Tney had it stated that he had made ample allowance for heroind the neighbours were unanimous in saying that he was very kind to his wife. Perhaps the husband did not think she was so seriously ill at the time and had given way to his wife's desire not to have anyone in the house, if they thought that he had neglected his wife they would have to record a verdict of manslaughter, while on the other hand they, might return a verdict according to the medical testi- mony. After a brief consultation the jury decided that death was mined as stated in the medical evidence, rod that no blame whatever was attached to the husband.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Boarclswas held at the Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, present—Messrs. J. Brundrett (in the chair), S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., T. Lea, A. R. Norman, and S. Yar wood. together With the members of the Rural District Council, with Mr. Ashton (clerk) and Mr. G. Astlton (deputy clerk.) ADDITIONAL RENUMERATION. The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the payment to the clerk of the following amounts for extra services in acting during the year as clerk to the follow- ing parochial committees. c---Appleton, £25; Frodsham township. £25; lirodshaifl L-irdship, £lO and Hatton, £lO. The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the payment of £l2O to the Clerk for his servicts as clerk to the Union Assessment Committee during the past year, and of £35 for his services as clerk to the School Attendance Committee. THE NEW EDUCATION BILL. . The Gateshead Union directed the attention of the Guardians to clause 2 sub-clause 5 of the Education Bill, 1896. The Gateshead Union saw no reason what- ever to permit the care of poor children which is at present vested in Guardians being transferred either to the Education Department or the proposed new Education Authority.—A communication from the Union and Rural District Clerks' Associa- tion, drawing attention to various aspects of the EillCatiOn Bill was read.—Mr. Woodward moved and Mr. Wright seconded a resolution that the letters be referred to the Parliamentary Committee. The resolu- tion was carried. WORKHOUSE INIARRIAGES—A PECULtAR POINT. The Guardians of the parish of St. Johns, Hampstead, drew attention to the fact that a couple of aged inmates of their House got married and then claimed possession of one of the rooms, set apar.; for married couples. The Guardians felt that the rooms were not intended for such cases and that it was a dangerous precedent. They suggested that the Runcorn Union. should petition for an amendment of the law, that would enable Boards to deal with each case on its merits find grant or refuse a room to a married couple.—Ed ward Parry moved that the :12 atter be referred to the Parliamentary Committee. Mr. Aaron seconded and it was carried.' THE LADIES' COIpIITTEE,

Mrs. Nellie Norman, Lyndhurst, Higher Runcorn, wrote saying that she was upable to act on the Ladies' Visiting Committee. . THE QUESTION OF OUTSIDE SCHOOLS. The Clerk reported that he hall three applications for the post of . school misiless to the Board.—Mr. W00d.4 ward proposed that-the appointment of a school mistress shotild not be made, and that the. girls should be sent to the Board School, at Dutton. He thought from what he had seen of the children of the North wich Union that outside sChooling would tend to improve the children 'and on' that ground he moved that the appointment be'not made, and that steps he taken forth? girls to he sent to the Board Schools.—Mr. Wright, seconded on the same grounds.—Mr. Mclntyre supported the resolutions. He had always looked upon the children, as a sort of you. g p tupt r prisoners and he thought if they had a mete litierty, and were all -.wed to breathe the pure ' air of heaven outside those walls—not that he wished to sly anything against the treatment of the children by the Authority—and were allowed to sit side by side with children of parish schools, it would be much better. There might be some difficulty but there was none which could not he overcome. If they were sent to school it would necessitate someone to take,care of them but they would get FOMCON, as cheaply as they would a school mistress. Be looked forward to the time when not only the girls hut thtt boys would loin them in running through the lanes to, the schools at Sutton.—(Mr. Woodward Hear, hear.)— Admiral parry expressed himself in sympathy with the resolution but thought that, pending arrangements-tor the reception of the children of the school, something would have to be done.—The Clerk pointed out that the question was whether they should appoint a.school mis- tress.—Mr. Woodward then moved that the question of the education of the girls he referred to a small commit- tee and also gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the girls be sent to the Dutton Schools. —Mr:- Weir seconded and this was unanimously carried.—The committee chosen was made op by Messrs. Heywood, Yarweod, Cnadwie,k, Mclntyre, Wright, 'Stokes, Normsn Williams, Weir and Nondward. t This concluded the business of the Board.

div.head: EVERY PERSON'S FUTURE.
div.p: EVERY PERSON'S FUTURE.

Every person's future is, to a certain extent, in his own hand. Many a future which might have been bril- liant has been darkened by lack of the spirit of self-help. Many a home might have been gladdened by life and health and comfort, has been saddened by poverty, illness and death, in many cases wholly preventible. The spring and summer months are, from a sanitary point of view, among the most important of the year. Due care may now mean a healthy and happy summer and autumn, and robust constitution to meet the trials of next winter. Neglect may now mean a joyless sum- mer, a trying autumn, and a broken constitution to succumb under the attacks of any exceptional trial. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT BY tiOYS AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday morning, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Alderman Harrison and Mr. T. Bir- chall, Percy Mather (M. Friars'-gate, and James M. Kenrick (13), Cairo-st.,were charged with stealing from the candle works of John Burgess,sometime between the 8:h and 9th inst., 20Ibs. of fat, value 2. 61 Both boys pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable, in relatir.g the cir- cumstances of the theft, said that Robert Smith, em- ployed by Mr. Burgess, had durimg the last two months periodically missed quantities of animal fat from the premises. He noticed that a cellar window had been tampered with, and concealed himself on Friday evening in a position where he could watch the window, and about nine o'clock he saw the two defendants come stealthily over the wall on to the enclosed preinises,with a sack. They opened the cellar window, went down to the basement, filled the sack with fat, took it to another portion of the premises, and concealed it. Mr. Smith communicated with the police, and Detective-Sergeant Monaghan watched in company with Smith the greater part of Saturday. At 4.30 the lads came and got the sack of fat, and Mather lifted it over the wall and placed it upon the shoulders of his younger companion. Monaghan then followed them to the premises of a marine store dealer, named Clifton, where they disposed of the fat,as they had done before. They were taken into custody and charged and they admitted the theft.ln:the books of the marine-store dealer were found seven entries of fat being sold within about a month, all in Mather's name. In fairness to the latter he said they did not suggest that all the fat had came from Burgess's, as the lad's brother was a butcher and he had been in the habit of getting fat clandestinely from him. Neither of the defendants had been before the bench be- fore for theft but Mather was some years ago in the hands of the police for stealing a sum of money from his father, who refused to go on with the prosecution. He was the son of a widow and was, the Chief Constable be- lieved, to some extent beyond her control. Kenrick's father was the late manager for the Carriage Company and be had had some trouble with the boy but had not known him do anything of that description before. Mather's mother bad given an undertaking that if her son was not sent to gaol she would get him seat to sea or under more severe control. The bench severely ad- monished Mather and fined him £1 including costs and ordered Kenrick to receive 12 strokes of the birch,which the Chairman hoped would make him feel physically and =natty his degradation.

Geary was dis- missed, however, for 4, when the score had reached 17, and Cheshire soon followed with 15 to his credit.A nice catch by Barker disposed of Storer.who had been hitting rather freely, for a score of 21. Alderson and Clare seemed to bs going great guns now. Smyth contri- buted nothing, and Moore had only 2 to his credit. Hollis shortly after followed for 10, when the score had reached 60. Trevellick and Dr. Winter seemed to have stopped the gap and had raised the score to 94, when the doctor was dismissed for 12, and then Trevellick soon followed his partner with 26. Hoyle contributed the second cypher in the game, being bowled by Dennis,and Wallwork was run out for 2 runs. Dutton being not out for 12 for the total of 116. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON,
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON,
WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

Considering the tempting weather which prevailed on Sunday there was a fair attendance at the service of the above-named society. The Rev. John Davies. of Rish- ton, formerly of Warrington, presided. and gave an en- couraging account of the success ef the P.S.A. aociety in connection with his church at Rishton. He said he had great faith in the movement and believed that it was destined to accomplish a vast amount of goed.—Mr. G. J. Brown, of Warrington, delivered an admirable ad- dress on "Courageous decisiveness." He condemned I those individuals who were afraid to avow their prin- , ciples, and who always sheltered themselves behind the opinions of other people. He gave several illustrations from tho history of men who dared to stand alone for conscience sake,referring to similar instances in the pre- sent day which had taken place in Armenia.—Mr.T.Wal- lineton. in making the announcements said ha was pleased to report an improvement in the health of their president (Rev. J. Yonge). but it would probably be aline weeks before he would be able to take part in their meetings.—Mr. Hickman proposed, Mr. W. Beswick se- conded, and it was carried unanimously, that the secre- tary write to Mr. Yonge expressing the sympathy of the brotherhood with him in his severe illness. Miss F. Booth sang very effectively a solo entitled "The Chords of Life. Mr. T. Hawthorn and Mr.E. A. Jones also took part in the servioe.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, ETC.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, ETC.

CASSRLL AND CO.—There are few people we think, unacquainted with the annual supplement of the " Magazine of Art " illustrating the pictures in the latest Royal Academy Exhibition, and fewer still, who once acquainted, do not welcome each succeeding year's edition. For 1896 the pictures of the 128th exhibition are illustrated, and Part 1 is just out. The publishers announce that Sir John Millais, P.R.A., has given them permission to re- produce his new academy picture entitled " The Forerunner." This picture will be issued with Part 5 and will form a frontispiece to the complete volume. This year's pictures again occupy five parts and the issue is printed on paper of even a superior quality to that which has hitherto been used. "Royal Academy Pictures" forms the most complete and perfect representation of the Academy ever placed within reach of the public. Not only is the best work of the year in painting and scu,lp- ture mirrored in its pages,but the scale upon which the pictures are produced, and the manner in which they are rendered, give an idea of the original such as can be gathered from no other source. In the first part alone the works of over 40 artistes are reproduced. and there is no room for doubt that the publishers have excelled themselves this year in the production of this famous supple- ment.—The May number of the "Magazine of Art" is also of exceptional interest. It contains as its frontispiece an etching by Mr. R. W. Macbeth, A.K.A., after one of Mr. Dendy Sadler's popular pictures, entitled "The Top of the Hill" (never before published). A second plate is a photogra- vure reproduction of one of Madame Ronnera cat subjects, "Sir John." A facsimile reproduction of a Study in Chalk by Mr. T. C. Gotch, and a full-page wood engraving of Mr. Dendy Sadler's "A Hunting Morn," are additional attractions of the number. The principal contents include a speeial article on the Life and Work of Mr. Dendy Sadler, illustrated with reproductions of mans of his most notable works ; the opening article of a series dealing with "The Evil One in Art," by Mr. John Leyland, and illustrated by Mr. Archie MacGregor. Mr. W. M. Gilbert writes the text to a beautiful series of draw- ings by Mr. MacWhirter, R.A., of the Hebrides; "Sport in Art: Shooting" is continued by Mr. J. G. Millais. "The Coin of the Realm" is the title of a critical paper by Mr. Lewis F. Day on our current coinage, which is fully illustrated; Mr. R. Anning Bell illustrates Shakespeare's verse, "Take, oh take those lips away." The part concludes with the "Chronicle of Art," which contains among numerous other matters of interest reproductions of two pages from an MS. of lone of the late Lord Leighton's lec- tures.—ln " Cassell's Magazine" for May, Mr. Harry Furniss illustrates a capitally written article on "Big men at Play," dealing with the hobbies of the great ones of the earth. Another article, to which readers of the magazine will turn with in- terest, is " How I became a millionaire " by Mr. Andrew Carnegie. In a chatty manner the writer tells the story of his rise from the position of a " bobbin-boy ' to being the possessor of Cluny Castle, Badenoch. A CONSTABLR AND CO.—ln the Acme library published by this firm" An Engagement" by Sir ttobert Peel, Bart., should occupy a prominent position. It is a cleverly written, and amusing little story, relating the unusual device of a lover, anxious to be married, to induce an influential and willing, though dilatory, relative to see to his ad- vancement. This forms the whole foundation of the tale, interest in which is throughout well sustained. As a sample of the author's work, the book is ex- cellent, so natural are its situations, charactersoind dialogue. MACILILLA.N AND Co.—ln the earlier part of this year Macmillan's magazine contained a story entitled " a Bride Elect," which was without the name of its author. Each month the reader was more enthralled in the tale and likewise further speculative and anxious as to the name of the writer. The story concluded and no clue was forth- coming but this month Messrs. Macmillan and Co. have issued "A Bride Elect in book form and it is seen that the work is from the pen of Mr. Theodore Douglas. To him then is the credit due for the production of a story decidedly original, both in treatment and denouement. Early in the book a girl unaccountably disappears and from this point to her ultimate discovery a vein of mystery runs through each chapter. Suspicion of course falls upon the innocent, and the actual state of things is entirely unsuspected. The science of embalming is the life- study of one of the chief characters, and his desire for the furtherance of his knowledge and love for the lady which has disappeared,spurs him on to the committal of a deed which comes as a shock to the peruser of the narrative. Cleverly hidden is the finale of the plot, and the work throughout shows thoughtful preparation.—A new story of good promise commences in Macmillan's Magazine for this month.—No book is more worthy of a place among the Illustrated Standard Novels than Samuel Lover's" Handy Andy,"" a single work by which." says Mr. Chatles Whibley in his introduction, " the author will be remembered—a work which you read in childhood with delight, and re-read in less impressionable years with a certain admira- tion lt is a book of farce and irresponsibility, a rough and tumble from end to end." Heartily amusing are some of Andy's scrapes, and likewise cunningly invented. Henry M. Brock is the illustrator.—" Idylls of the King ° occupy two more parts of the rennysouian People's edition, and these have just been issued, making the 13th and 14th respectively ot these chaste little books.—A biography of Cardinal Richelieu by Richard Lodge, M.A., proves very interesting read- ing. Richelieu was a striking personality, and in his time almost a swayer of destinies. His politi-

cal power was unrivalled, and his influence equally great. In the elder Dumas' novels a great deal is learnt about him, and enough interest stimulated with regard to him to make this biography wel- come. It is complete, and follows the career of the great French statesman step by step. GEORGE NEWER!!! AND CO.—" Round London," an album of pictures from photographs of the chief places of interest in and around London, is now complete, and well worth binding by those who have it, or procuring by those who have not. THE TECHNICAL PUBLISHING Co, LTD.—In this week's issue of" The Practical Engineer" there is commenced a serial story entitled "The Naval En- gineer and the Command of the Sea," a story of , naval administration by Francis G. Burton- Tbe story is written specially for this journal with the object of illustrating the important part which will be played by the Engineering Staff in ships of war in future naval engagements, and with a view to pointing out the disabilities under which its mem- bers at present labour. The question is one of con- siderable public importance, inasmuch as the sense of injustice which prevails amongst engineers, with regard to the treatment meted out to this section of , the service, militates against its popularity, and in the event of any outbreak of hostilities would seri- ously impair the efficiency of what is rightly re- garded as our" First line of Defence." The ven- ture is a laudable one and should commend itself to all readers with a sense of the necessity for uphold- ing England's supremacy. As far as we can judge, the story is written in an interesting way, and not too technical.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

The traffic on the Ship Canal last week showed an Increase of 3,285 net registered tons as compared with the returns of the preceding week. The Cork Steam- ship Company's new weekly service to Boulogne was inaugurated by the departure of the steamer Bittern on Thursday morning with general merchandise and 100 tons of coal. A new service between Manchester Waterford,and Cork will be started on Wednesday next, when the screw steamer. Liverpool, 213 tons net, wil leave No. 2 Dock, Pomona, for Ireland. INCREASED SALT SHIPMENTS FROM THE CANAL A return of the exports of salt from the Mersey shows that, while there has been a more or less steady dim- inution in the Liverpool shipments as compared with last year, the salt trade of the Ship Canal continues to increase. During April the total shipments from the Mersey were 49.217 tons, compared with 48,879 tons in April, 1895. Of these 36,852 tons were shipped from Liverpool (compered with 37,094) and 12,365 tons from Runcorn and Weston Point (compared with 11,785 tons). The total shipments ter the first quarter of this year amounted to 103,128 tons, compared with 114,419 tons in the corresponding period of 1895. Of this total 83,600 tons were shipped from Liverpool (compared with 102,724 tons last year) and 19,528 from Runcorn and Weston (compared with 11,695 tons). It will thus be seen that, whereas the salt exports from Liverpool during the first quarter of 1896 showed a falling off of 19 per cent„ the exports from the Ship Canal increased during the same period by 87 per cent.

With width of only two windows on the ground floor, and 0, three above, it ranks almost as a cottage beside the CO parative palaces occupied by Lily, Duchess of Mar borough, or by Mr. Astor, within a stone's-throw of the Carlton. An equal absence of ostentation seems 11kalf4 to mark the habits and manners of the youngest a 13,1 richest of American duchesses throughout the season. 11 a later period the duke and duchess will no doubt rno/.0 into quarters commensurate with their great weal for it is said to be one of the dreams of the duchess r..° restore Marlborough House to the family that was Ori merly too poor to maintain it. div.head: WARRINGTON BIGAMY CASE.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BIGAMY CASE.
SEVERE SENTENCE AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.

On Thursday week,Harriet Annie Ellis was indicted at the Liverpool Assizes before Mr. Justice Grantham for having committed bigamy by marrying Charles Lewis Geddes, at Runcorn, her husband Charles Henry Ellis being then alive. The defendant pleaded that she did not marry with the intention of doing any harm, and the learned Judge directed that a plea of" not guilty " be entered. Mr. Collingwood Hope, instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the prosecution and related the facts as detailed at the Warrington Police Court when prisoner was committed. The defendant in reply to the Judge said that her husband when he left her at Ellesmere Port told her that his mother load consulted a solicitor who had advised her that the marriage was an illegal one and that she could go and do whatever she thcught fit, by marrying again or otherwise, as the form of marriage they had gone through at Stoalc Parish Church was not binding, as they were both infants and had been married under wrong names. It was quite true that she had heard from her husband after he had enlisted in the army and whilst in India, but he always addressed her as Miss Wilkinson. That happened before her marriage with ' Geddes and therefore when she went through the form of marriage with him she did not know she was doing any harm. His Lordship questioned Detective Sergeant Monaghan and after seeing that the certificate of -narriage, had the p isoner's mother's signature as a witness he told her that what she had said was no justification whatever as the marriage was a perfectly binding one until set aside. After summing up and the jury finding prisoner guilty, his Lordship said in his opinion the case was a very ser- ious one, and one that called for severe punishment in- asmuch as prisoner had gone through a proper form of marriage and ought not to have deceived Mr. Geddes, who had behaved very well all throughout. He could not pass a lighter sentence than three months with hard labour.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1896. MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL. AT EAR.LESTOWN.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1896. MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL. AT EAR.LESTOWN.
THE MISSING RUNCORN CAPTAIN.
AN IMPOSING ARRAY. EXCITING INCIDEN TS.

The annual ceremony of crowning the May Queen was brought off with complete success at Earlestown en Saturday. From early morning the town wore a gay and festive appearance,this'peing more marked in E trle- street, Market-street, and Bridge street, while Queen-st. was entirely devoid of decoration. The children were soon astir, and could be seen flitting hero and there eagerly anticipating the grand disptay in which they were to take an important part. As.on previous occa- sions the marshalling ground was a field 'belonging to Mr. T. Molyneux, near Vitriol-square, and about one o'clock the children in multifarious costumes .began to wend their way to the rendezvous. Thefday was beau- tifully fine,but it could be plainly seen that much incon- venience would arise from the dust which would be raised by the procession. It- was hoped however that the township authorities would turn out the water cart, and carry on a, process of watering the streets somewhat prior to the time of starting. Any hopes which were entertained in this direction were dkpelled, for the dust continued to fly about in clouds all the afternoon. Several prizes were Offered for the neatest and cleanest turnouts of horses and conveyances which were intended to take part in the procession. The competitors mustered at the Vitriol-square, and owing to the large number which entered there was an exceedingly good show. Messrs. Gilbert and Abbott were th'e judges, and after carefully examining all the competing animals and vehicles tdey awarded the prizes as follows :—Class A.- The neatest and cleanest turnout at the disposal of the committee. Ist prize £l. Messrs. J. Fairclough and Sons (driver J. H. Clarke) ; 2nd prize 155., Stnkey Sugar Company (driver J. Dutton) ; 3rd priz3 103., Mr. J. Cawley—there were ten entries. Class B, for the neatest ,and cleanest tradesman's turhout :-Ist prie,, £l, S. Bethell (driver. G.' Green) ; 2nd prize, 3.53., E. L. Bent ; 3rd prize, 10s., Mr. M. Winstanley. There were 18 entries. Mr, Mark- land Offered special prizes for the cleanest vehicle in the procession :-Ist prize, 153., Mr. T. Molyneux ; 2nd prize,Mr.MacD rtnott ; 3rd prize, Mr. M Winstanley.Mr. Alderson also offered a special prize of two guineas for the best and neatest turnout, the bona-fide property of a tradesman in the district. This was won by Mr. S. Bethell. At the conclusion of the judging all the vehicles drove on to the marshalling ground to take up their

The marshalls were Messrs. J.Burrows and J.Wadding- ton, and their task, although they were ably, assisted by members of the committee, was by no me.ins an envi- able one. Although the time for assembly was fixed at 1.30, children continued to arrive for fully an hour afterwards, and it was not until nearly 3.30 that the heterogeneous mass was got into something like order, and a move was made. The precession was headed by heChairman (Rev. T. R. Matthews) in a coriveyanee, and the route traversed was via Queen-st., Faiiclough- street, Bridge-street, Market-street, Legh-street,Sankey- strret, Regent-street, Viaduct-street, returning by way of Earle-street, and Market-street, to the Grand Stand on Newton race course.

The streets were packed with crowds of sightseers, many of whom had come from Warrington, St. Helens and surrounding districts, but admirable order was kept. by a special staff of police under the charge of Inspec- tor Morgan and Sergeant Clarke. The starting of the procession was slightly marred by an accident to two lads named Baston and Nunnerley. The boys were seated on a lorry with their legs over the side, and in , leaving the field the horse turned rather sharply. and the lurry coming against the gate post, the legs of. both lads were crushed, fortunately, however, no bones were broken, and the lads are now progressing nicely. Tne procession was most imposing,and it was evident to every- one that the parents must have expended a considerable amount of time and labour in preparing the children. The characters represented were something similar to previous years, but thee were several additional and new characters. After the flower girls came Robin Hood (W. Slinn) on horseback, Maid Marian (bl. Taberner) and a retinue of foresters ; more flower girls and a lurry with " Poppy " (M. A. Pilling), Wild Rose (E. Johnson). There was then a quick transfer frem the sublithe to the ridiculous, for immediately following these came a motley crew in all manner of costumes and get-up, and faces paint, din various colours who called , themselves the " Serewing shop" band. They were all lads fit for anything, and the musieal instruments they carried included a big drum, tin whistles, banjos, con- certinas and such like. They seem to enjoy themselves. Another pleasant change was a lurry with Cupid (L. Slinn), Queen of Hearts (F. Morris), Queen of Diamonds , (M. Siddeley), Queen of Clubs (M. Brown). Queen of Spades (L. Beron), with their maids B. Mitchell. E. Baron, M. Mitchell. and R. S mister ; music. K, Holde- worth and Elisier leiraYnaicf(L. Diekinson). The Eerles- town prize band interposed here,aud they were followed by the floral dancers charmingly attired in lemon and blue coloured frocks with hats to match, and the May pole dancers 41 white with pink trimmings, all of them, being in charge of Mr. G. Slinn. There followed after- wards the usual attributes, such as farmers and plough- men, bakers, colliers, Red Rieing Hoods, nurses, joiners, cripketers, gipsy boys and girls, &c., but the principal characters . were • 80-peep (Edith- Haskins), Boy Blue .(Master Walker), Prince (J. Goodwin), Cinderella (Miss Lythgoe), Queen Elizabeth (Edith Elemmons) Bopeep (Sissie Naylor) and lamb; School- for Scandal (Misses Ogden. Singleton, and Barnes), Prince Charming (F. Owen), Up-to-Date (H. Owen), jockey (H. Peplew), two little girls in blue (El. and A. Owen), Cherry Ripe (H. Owen), Queen Rosebud (Miss Holdsworth), White Slave (Miss Brown), Ex-Queen (Miss Thompson) ; J. Camm's tobacco agent (an excellent make-up). Britannia (Miss Crowther), John Bull (A. Porter) ,Ireland (J. Richardson), Scotland (Coombs),e% ales (Amy Howarth), sword bearer (N. Stevens), sceptre bearer (Percy Horridge), mimic archbishop (A. Joves). The conveyance, dra.wn'by two horses, containing the Queen (Miss Edith Plant) brought up the rear of the precession. She looked exceedingly pretty and was at- tired tail heliotrope satin dress and carried an immense bouqu'llt'of fhwers. ' She was 'escorted by a detachment of South Lancashire Volunteers under Sergeant Bailey. tier paees were .(Masters Meyricks and Payne), train bearers (Mullins and Pidceck). maids of honour (Amy Watson, Lillie Travis, Mary Skidmore, May Green, Eliza A. Caldwell, and Susan E. Warren.) A striking feature in the procession was Walton and Co's Flint glass hands who carried splendid specimens of their handicraft. The other bands present were tke Liverpool Farm School band, which headed Messrs. Berron and Co's., glass bottle makers, and the Golborne• brass band. On arrival at the Grand Stand, the ceremony of Crowning the Queen was proceeded with, the process being witnessed by a very large crowd of people. The important duty of proclaiming Miss Plant, Queen of the May, was performed by Mrs. F..J. Emmett, who after- wards made the Queen a presentation. The other items on the programme included an exhibition of strength by Peter Mack, May pale and floral dances, drill and exer- cise lay Scotch Highlanders, bayonet exercise and physical chill by Guard of Honour, and dancing by the U-po-bo dancers. The performance of these lads was really remarkable, and they v are vociferously applauded. Just before the coronation ceremony the conveyance which had brought Mrs. Emmett was being drawn clear, when the wheel caught the platform causing the carriage to swerve, and a large number of people were in immin- ent danger until it was happily averted. One woman, however, had a foot injured by one of the horses stepping upon it. The arrangements were satisfactorily carried out by committee consisting of.Messrs.J. Lowe, S. Openshaw, W. Baston, J. Burrows, H. Crowther. T. Latimer, G. Payne, C. Hamblett, J. Clark, W. Lanwarne and J. Barcroft, with Mr. J. Waddington as secretary.
A. NEWTON CASE AT THE ASSIZES. COMPENSATION FOR TEIE LOSS OF A SON.

WILLIAMS V. THE LONDON AND NORTEUWESTERN RAIL- WAY COMPANY—This was an action brought,. at the Liverpool Assiv?s on Saturday, by Mrs. Ann Williams, widow, for compensation for the loss of a son owing to the alleged negligence of servants of the defendant com- pany. Mr. Shee, Q.C., and Mr. Horridge were for the plaintiff ; and Mr. l'ickford, Q.C., and Mr. Saunderson represented the defendants. For a considerable period prior to 127 h December last Herbert Smith Williams, the deeased man, was employed at the Vulcan Iron Foun- dry, Wargrave, Newton-le-Willows, the works of which' adjoined the London and North-western Railway. For seine distance a siding rens parallel with the defendant company's main line. On the 12th December four loaded waggons arrived, and were shunted into the siding lead- ing into the Vulcan premises, and ahead of the position occupied by nine empty waggons, which had previously been drawn out. From the evidence of witnesses in support of plaintiff's case, the waggotas were sent into the siding at the rate of ten or twelve miles an hour. Efforts were made to check their progress by two of the foundry brakemen, who used the brakes, but without avail, for the waggons crushed through the doors of the smith's stoop and into the forge. The man Williams,who was 38 years of age, and an engine fitter, was passing through the premises at the time, and he was caught by the waggons, and so badly injured that he died on the Sunday following. The deceased had for a long time been the sole support of his widowed mother, Ann Wil- liams, to whom he gave 30g. a week for housekeeping purposes, the family consisting of three.—Mr. Pickforcl, for the defence, submitted that no negligence had been shown on the part of the em- ployees of the railway company. The shunting of the waggons into the Vulcan Foundry pre- mises was carried out under the instructions of Thomas Sankey, brakestnan in the employ of the foundry com- pany. He gave orders that the waggons were to be sent into the yard sharper than they had pteviously been sent there. That being so, the defendants' servants had every right to conclude that Sankey had seen to the opening of the doors of toe forndry, and the ordering of all persons out of danger. No blame &r the accident Could be attached to the railway men.—The witnesses called for the defence stated that, in their opinion, the waggons were only tiavelling at the rate of five or six miles an hour, and that after the engine had been stopped Sankey signalled for the driver to go on.—The jury after consultation in private, found for the plain- tiff, awarding the mother £250.
